objects.definition: A model of three overlapping ways to understand and teach student writing: study skills (writing as a transferable individual skill), academic socialisation (learning a discipline's stable discourses and genres) and academic literacies (writing as social practice bound up with meaning making, identity, power and what counts as knowledge in an institution). Reach for it to diagnose the assumptions behind writing support, to design teaching that makes genre and mode shifts explicit without treating students as deficient, and to engage staff as writers. It is not a teaching method with steps: its authors offer it as a design frame, and critics say its pedagogy is unclear.
objects.extendedDefinition: Mary Lea and Brian Street proposed the three models in a study of student writing in UK universities (*Studies in Higher Education*, 1998) and restated them, with two worked applications, in *Theory Into Practice* (2006) [D:LS2006, p. 368; D:LS1998, not read]. The study skills model treats writing as an individual, cognitive skill; academic socialisation treats it as acculturation into a discipline's discourses and genres; academic literacies treats it as social practice involving meaning making, identity, power and authority; it asks what counts as knowledge in each context [D:LS2006, pp. 368-369]. The authors say the models overlap and are not mutually exclusive, and that the first two have guided most curriculum and research [D:LS2006, p. 369]. Its main use is as a frame for writing development and course design that challenges a deficit view of students [D:LS2006, pp. 368, 376]. Its disputes: whether the models are a hierarchy or nested, and whether academic literacies yields a workable pedagogy [D:DW2024].

objects.definition: Wingate's case for teaching academic literacy inside every discipline's curriculum, through collaboration between EAP or learning development specialists and subject lecturers, using genre analysis of student texts, six ways to embed it in ordinary teaching and staff development for lecturers. Reach for it to design or argue for embedded academic literacy provision, to plan collaboration between a library or skills team and a department, or to critique generic study skills provision. It is not a theory of what literacy is: for that, use Lea and Street's academic literacies model.
objects.extendedDefinition: Ursula Wingate, of King's College London, set out in a 2015 plenary, published in 2016 and 2018, that academic literacy, the ability to communicate competently in a discipline's discourse community, must be taught to all students within the curriculum [D:WG2018, pp. 349-350]. She argues that the dominant provision, generic EAP and study skills courses outside the disciplines, is remedial, rests on misconceptions of students' needs and misallocates responsibility away from subject lecturers [D:WG2018, pp. 350-351]. She reports a genre-based writing intervention built with subject lecturers, a PGCAP module that taught six ways to embed literacy in teaching, and the Australian curriculum-integrated model [D:WG2018, pp. 353-361]. She concludes that effective support needs three things: curriculum embedding, genre analysis and collaboration between EAP and subject specialists [D:WG2018, p. 362]. Her own limits: the intervention was additional rather than embedded, collaboration was hard to sustain and no performance data was gathered [D:WG2018, p. 358].

objects.definition: A behavioural therapy that aims to increase psychological flexibility: making room for difficult thoughts and feelings rather than fighting them, and acting on chosen values. Reach for it to describe or explain the ACT model, its six processes and its tools. Not for choosing anyone's treatment, and not as a self-help programme in itself.
objects.extendedDefinition: Developed by Steven Hayes, Kirk Strosahl and Kelly Wilson (first book 1999; second edition 2012), ACT is one of the third-wave behaviour therapies [D:CUL2008]. It rests on functional contextualism and relational frame theory, a behavioural account of language and cognition [D:HAY2006]. Its aim is psychological flexibility: contacting the present moment fully and changing or persisting in behaviour when that serves one's values. Six linked processes build it: acceptance, cognitive defusion, contact with the present moment, self as context, values and committed action [D:HAY2006; D:ZHA2018]. A review of 20 meta-analyses found it efficacious for anxiety, depression, substance use, pain and mixed groups, though not consistently better than CBT [D:GLO2020]. The main dispute is how strong that evidence is: a stricter meta-analysis judged it not yet well established for any disorder [D:OST2014]. NICE names it, with CBT, among the psychological therapies for chronic primary pain [D:NICE2021].

objects.term: Student access retention attainment and progression framework
aliases: student access retention attainment and progression framework
Advance HE access retention attainment progression
objects.definition: A short sector framework that sets out what students need to get into, stay in, succeed in and move on from higher education, as three dials (institution, educators and related staff, students), each quartered by the four lifecycle stages of access, retention, attainment and progression, with 49 named segments in all. Reach for it to map support across the student journey, to open a conversation with staff or students about one stage of that journey or to link student success work to PSF evidence (Part F gives the dialogue). It is not a measure of success or a method for closing awarding gaps: it gives no procedure, data or evidence base.
objects.extendedDefinition: Advance HE published the framework in 2024 as one of its Student Success Frameworks [D:AHE24S, p. 2]. It defines four interconnected elements of a successful student journey (access, retention, attainment and progression), each resting on belonging and active engagement, and takes a holistic view that includes wellbeing and personal development [D:AHE24S, p. 2]. It assigns responsibility to senior leaders, staff and students together [D:AHE24S, p. 3], grounds the case in providers' legal, ethical and economic duties [D:AHE24S, p. 4] and views the subject from three nested perspectives, each drawn as a dial of named segments sorted by stage [D:AHE24S, pp. 5-11]. It gives each perspective a short list of uses [D:AHE24S, pp. 12-13] and names ten PSF dimensions it serves [D:AHE24S, p. 14]. Its main tension is how it frames students: as people in need of support (remedial support appears on the students' dial) and as partners who share responsibility, while it names awarding gaps without saying how to close them [D:AHE24S, pp. 3-4, 11].

objects.definition: The generic five-phase frame for designing instruction: analysis, design, development, implementation and evaluation, sequential but also iterative. Reach for it to name the phases of an instructional development project and to plan the work and outputs of each. It is not an authored model with fixed rules: beyond the five names, what ADDIE "says" varies by source, so cite the specific version in use.
objects.extendedDefinition: ADDIE names five processes of instructional systems development: analysis, design, development, implementation and evaluation [D:MOL2003]. Molenda found no original source: the acronym spread by word of mouth from the late 1980s, and its nearest forerunner is IPISD, built by Florida State University's Center for Educational Technology for the US military in the mid-1970s, whose phases were analyse, design, develop, implement and control [D:MOL2003; D:BRA1975, not read]. It is used as an umbrella for systematic instructional and training design in universities and workplaces [D:PSU; D:OBE2022]. Its disputes: whether it is linear and slow (the critics) or iterative (its defenders); and whether, lacking an authoritative text, it is a model at all [D:MOL2003; D:PSU; D:OBE2022].

objects.definition: A five-element model of what each person needs to go through a change: awareness of the need, desire to take part, knowledge of how, ability to do it and reinforcement to keep it up, each decided by named factors. Reach for it to plan, check or diagnose the people side of a change, one person or group at a time, by finding the barrier point, the first element that is weak. Not a prescribed change process and not an independently tested theory: its author presents it as a framework, and its evidence is the issuer's own benchmarking.
objects.extendedDefinition: Jeffrey Hiatt, founder of Prosci, set out ADKAR in his book of 2006 after about ten years developing it from Prosci's benchmarking of change projects [D:H2006, preface; p. 143]. It began as a question asked of every change management tactic: what result is it for? Mapping tactics to their results gave five building blocks: awareness, desire, knowledge, ability and reinforcement [D:H2006, preface]. The elements fall in the order one person experiences change, are cumulative and must all be present for a change to be realised; the first weak element is the barrier point, where effort goes next [D:H2006, pp. 1, 3, 60]. Hiatt gives five uses: teaching change management, checking change plans, coaching by managers, assessing changes under way and planning [D:H2006, p. 131]. It is widely used, including in nursing and health informatics [D:KAM2022]. (editorial) Its main limit is evidence: the book supports the model with case studies and Prosci's own survey data, not a test of the model itself.

objects.definition: A hierarchical classification of educational objectives about interests, attitudes, values and character, in five levels and thirteen subcategories ordered by internalisation: receiving, responding, valuing, organisation and characterisation by a value or value complex. Reach for it to make vague affective aims ("appreciate", "be interested in") specific, to sequence them and to judge what a test item can show. It is not a measure of a person: its authors say the boundaries are arbitrary and that affective outcomes are slow to show and hard to grade fairly.
objects.extendedDefinition: Published in June 1964 by David Krathwohl, Benjamin Bloom and Bertram Masia as Handbook II of the Taxonomy of Educational Objectives, after the cognitive handbook of 1956 [D:KBM1964, copyright page; D:K2002, p. 218]. Its organising principle is internalisation, the process by which a value moves from bare awareness to a pervasive outlook that guides behaviour [D:KBM1964, pp. 27-28, 33]. The authors built it because affective aims erode from courses, being hard to grade, slow to show and confused with indoctrination [D:KBM1964, pp. 15-20]. It is used to write outcomes about attitudes and values, above all in professional programmes such as nursing [D:SN2025]. Its disputes: whether values can be arranged in a hierarchy at all, and how to assess them [D:SN2025; D:GP2010]; the authors themselves are less sure of the subcategories than of the five levels [D:KBM1964, p. 33].

objects.definition: A short declaration of four values and twelve principles for developing software, written in 2001 by seventeen practitioners of lightweight methods. Reach for it to describe what "agile" means at its source, or to judge whether a practice fits that meaning. It is not a method: it prescribes no process, roles or artefacts.
objects.extendedDefinition: Seventeen people representing Extreme Programming, Scrum, DSDM, Adaptive Software Development, Crystal, Feature-Driven Development, Pragmatic Programming and others met at Snowbird, Utah, on 11 to 13 February 2001, signed the manifesto and formed the Agile Alliance [D:HIS2001]. It values individuals and interactions, working software, customer collaboration and responding to change over processes and tools, comprehensive documentation, contract negotiation and following a plan, while granting the latter value [D:AM2001]. Twelve principles follow [D:AMP2001]. It became the reference point for a decade of research [D:DIN2012]. (editorial) Its main dispute is what has been done in its name: whether the industry that grew around "agile" keeps to its values.

objects.term: Deep and surface approaches to learning
aliases: deep and surface approaches to learning
objects.definition: The idea, from Marton and Säljö's Gothenburg studies of 1976, that students attend either to the surface of a task (the words, facts and figures to reproduce) or to its meaning (what the author intends), that this choice follows what they think the task requires, and that the quality of what they learn follows the choice. Reach for it to explain why assessment and task design shape how students study, to read students' answers for qualitative differences, and to frame the deep and surface pair that later questionnaires and constructive alignment build on. It is not a classification of students: an approach is a response to a task in a context, never a fixed trait.
objects.extendedDefinition: Ference Marton and Roger Säljö, at the Institute of Education of the University of Gothenburg, set out the distinction in two linked papers in the British Journal of Educational Psychology in 1976 [D:MS1976a (recall); D:MS1976b]. A learner's attention can rest on the surface of a text, the sign, or on its intentional content, what the sign stands for; they called these surface-level and deep-level processing [D:MS1976b, p. 117]. Part II showed that forty first-term students adapted their way of learning to what the questions they met led them to expect, and that predictable demands could turn even meaning-oriented questions into a routine, which they called technification [D:MS1976b, pp. 117, 121-125]. They described outcomes as qualitatively different conceptions of the same content, set out as an outcome space [D:MS1976b, pp. 116, 118]. Later writers, the authors among them, renamed the pair deep and surface approaches, and Entwistle, Ramsden and Biggs built questionnaires and models on it [D:EOL2005; D:BKL2001]. Its main use is to argue that assessment shapes learning; its main disputes are whether so simple a pair can bear both a teaching metaphor and a research construct [D:TOR2014], how consistently deep processing predicts better performance [D:DA2012] and whether students' approaches deepen over a degree [D:AG2017].

objects.definition: A curriculum design framework that plans backwards from results: first the desired results (transfer goals, understandings, essential questions, knowledge and skills), then the evidence that would show them (performance tasks judged by six facets of understanding, plus other evidence), then the learning plan (acquisition, meaning making and transfer). Reach for it to design a unit, module or course so that teaching and assessment serve agreed results, and to avoid activity-led or coverage-led teaching. It is not a theory of how people learn, and it is weaker where outcomes should emerge rather than be set in advance.
objects.extendedDefinition: Grant Wiggins and Jay McTighe set out Understanding by Design in a book published by ASCD (1998; expanded 2nd edn 2005) and in later guides and a white paper (2014) [D:MW2014; D:WM1998, not read; D:WM2005, not read]. Design runs backwards in three stages: identify desired results, determine acceptable evidence, then plan learning experiences and instruction [D:MW2014]. Understanding is shown by transfer and judged through six facets (explain, interpret, apply, perspective, empathy, self-knowledge); teaching serves three goals: acquisition, meaning making and transfer [D:MW2014]. It is widely used for school curriculum and has been applied in university course design [D:ML2016]. Its disputes: setting outcomes in advance may narrow what students learn, and the process takes time and expert support [D:HEI2019; D:ML2016].

aliases: brief behavioural activation treatment for depression
objects.definition: A structured, time-limited behavioural therapy for depression that helps people act according to a plan rather than their mood, so they re-engage with activities that bring natural reward and stop the avoidance that keeps depression going. Reach for it to describe or explain BA's model, principles and techniques. Not for choosing anyone's treatment.
objects.extendedDefinition: BA grew from Lewinsohn's behavioural theory of depression (1974) and his treatment manual of 1976 [D:KAN2010, p. 609], and from Jacobson and colleagues' component analysis of cognitive therapy (1996), which found that adding cognitive techniques to the behavioural ones did not improve outcomes [D:KAN2010, p. 610]. Martell, Addis and Jacobson then set out BA as a treatment in its own right (2001), and Martell, Dimidjian and Herman-Dunn gave its ten core principles in their clinician's guide (2010; second edition 2022) [D:KAN2010, p. 610; D:MDH2022, p. 22]. It treats depression as following life problems that reduce positive reward, kept going by avoidance, and works by scheduling activity and testing it [D:MDH2022, pp. 20, 23]. In a large trial it did as well as medication and better than cognitive therapy for more severe depression [D:KAN2010, p. 610]; meta-analysis finds a large effect against controls [D:EKE2014], and it was no worse than CBT delivered by junior workers [D:RIC2016]. Its main dispute is which of its many components do the work: activity monitoring and scheduling are constant across versions, and which others are needed is unknown [D:KAN2010, pp. 608, 616]. [P2, 2 Oct: history and dispute now from KAN2010.]

objects.definition: A structured, time-sensitive talking therapy built on the cognitive model: how people interpret situations shapes how they feel, act and react in the body; learning to evaluate thinking more realistically eases distress. Reach for it to describe or explain CBT, its model of thoughts and beliefs, its principles, its terms and the shape of a course and a session of therapy; not to give therapy, diagnose or advise on anyone's treatment.
objects.extendedDefinition: Aaron T. Beck developed cognitive therapy for depression in the 1960s and 1970s; the name is often used interchangeably with cognitive behaviour therapy [D:JB2021, p. 3]. Its cognitive model holds that dysfunctional thinking, which shapes mood and behaviour, is common to psychological disturbances, and that cognition works at three levels: automatic thoughts, intermediate beliefs and core beliefs [D:JB2021, pp. 4-5]. Treatment rests on an evolving cognitive conceptualization and fourteen principles, among them collaboration, structured sessions, guided discovery and Action Plans between sessions [D:JB2021, pp. 16-24]. The third edition adds a recovery-oriented, strengths-based emphasis (CT-R) [D:JB2021, pp. 7-8]. UK guidance recommends it for depression [D:NICE2022, tables 1 and 2, pp. 31-35, 49-50]; a meta-review of 494 systematic reviews found modest benefit across conditions, mostly against inactive comparisons [D:FOR2021]. Its disputes: the size and durability of its effects [D:FOR2021; D:CR2017], and whether it attends enough to culture, power and the social causes of distress [D:JB2021, p. 18; D:PAL2018].

objects.definition: A theory that children build their own understanding by acting on the world, adapting their mental schemata through assimilation and accommodation, and passing through four stages of thinking from sensorimotor to formal operational, the first of them in six sensorimotor stages. Reach for it to explain constructivist, discovery and readiness-based teaching, and as the root of later stage and level schemes (SOLO's modes, Kolb's learning). It is not a reliable timetable for what a given child can do: its ages and its universality are disputed.
objects.extendedDefinition: Jean Piaget (1896-1980), working in Geneva from the 1920s with Bärbel Inhelder and others, proposed that intelligence develops as the child constructs knowledge through action [D:BRIT; D:BAR2015]. In *The origins of intelligence* (1936) he treats intelligence as an extension of biological adaptation, an equilibrium between assimilating things to the subject's schemata and accommodating the schemata to things, and traces it through six stages of sensorimotor intelligence in the first two years [D:P1936, pp. 3-7, 147-152]. Development then runs through four periods (sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational), each underpinned by logical structures [D:BAR2015; D:MCL]. It shaped child-centred, discovery and readiness-based teaching [D:MCL; D:WIKI]. Its disputes: children show competences earlier than Piaget held, development is uneven across domains, and the theory gave little place to culture, language and social interaction [D:BAR2015; D:BAB2019; D:MCL]; defenders argue many criticisms rest on a *standard interpretation* of the theory [D:LOU1998; D:BEB2021].

objects.definition: The UK's standard subject classification for higher education data: HECoS gives 1,092 defined subject codes; the Common Aggregation Hierarchy (CAH) groups them in three levels (21 broad subject areas, 35 subject groups and 166 to 167 detailed subject groups). Reach for it to place a course, benchmark or standard in a subject grouping, to aggregate subject data consistently, or as the model for META's own knowledge hierarchy. It is not a map of ideas or theories: it classifies subjects of study, not knowledge within them.
objects.extendedDefinition: HESA, with the UK sector, introduced the Higher Education Classification of Subjects (HECoS) and its Common Aggregation Hierarchy (CAH) to replace JACS, applying them to data from 2019/20 [D:HARC, summary]. HECoS is a flat vocabulary of subject terms; in the held version each of its 1,092 terms has a six-digit code, a definition, often a scope note, non-preferred terms and related terms, and one CAH3 parent [D:HECD]. CAH aggregates those codes upwards in three levels so that subject data can be analysed consistently [D:CAHD; D:HMG2, summary]. The guide sets structural rules (every level covers all of HECoS; a parent with one child shares its title) and governs change through a steering group, an advisory panel and HESA's management office, with at least a year's notice of substantive change [D:HMG2, summary]. The main limits are practical: subjects missing from the vocabulary (no CAH3 group for criminology or project management, as ADAPT found) and version drift between the 167 groups HESA states and the 166 in the held file [D:CAHD].

objects.definition: A principle for designing teaching: state what students should be able to do as a verb, an object and a context; have them enact that verb in the teaching and learning activities; assess whether and how well they can with tasks that need the same verb; grade against criteria, not against each other. Reach for it to design or audit a course or programme so that outcomes, activities and assessment fit; also to map course outcomes to programme and graduate outcomes. It is not a taxonomy of levels in itself: Biggs pairs it with SOLO.
objects.extendedDefinition: John Biggs proposed constructive alignment in 1996, from a course for in-service teachers at the University of Hong Kong assessed by portfolio, and developed it in Teaching for Quality Learning at University (1999; with Catherine Tang from 2007; 4th edn 2011) [D:B1996, pp. 347, 352; D:BT2011, pp. 95-97]. It rests on twin principles: constructivism, that learners construct knowledge through their own activity, and alignment of the teaching and of the assessment tasks to the intended learning outcomes [D:BT2011, pp. 97, 108]. Design runs in four stages: describe each outcome as a verb, its object and a context and standard; create teaching and learning activities that address the verb; use assessment tasks that contain the verb, judged with rubrics; turn the judgements into grades [D:BT2011, p. 100]. Outcomes are set at three levels (graduate, programme and course) and aligned by curriculum mapping [D:BT2011, pp. 113, 127-130]. It is used across university teaching and is written into quality frameworks in the UK, Hong Kong and Europe [D:BT2011, pp. 306-307; D:LLL2021, p. 122]. Its disputes: whether outcome statements carry the precision claimed for them [D:HS2002, pp. 225-227], whether its adoption by policy has kept the alignment and dropped the constructivism [D:LLL2021, pp. 124-127]; and how far its evidence comes from its authors and their colleagues [D:BT2011, pp. 306-309].

objects.definition: A framework that replaces critical thinking with critical being: criticality in three domains (knowledge, the self, the world), each with its form (critical reason, critical self-reflection, critical action), at four levels from critical skills to transformatory critique, integrated in the critical person. Reach for it to argue that being critical is a disposition of the whole person, to place a course's criticality on the grid and to plan a curriculum that reaches the higher levels in all three domains. It is not a test or a list of critical thinking skills: Barnett treats skills as the lowest level only.
objects.extendedDefinition: Ronald Barnett set out critical being in *Higher education: a critical business* (SRHE and Open University Press, 1997) [D:B1997]. He argues that higher education has no proper account of critical thinking and has confined it to formal knowledge at instrumental levels, and that it should be replaced by the wider concept of critical being, which embraces critical thinking, critical action and critical self-reflection [D:B1997, pp. 1-2, 7]. Criticality runs on two axes: three domains (knowledge, the self, the world) and four levels (critical skills, reflexivity, refashioning of traditions, transformatory critique), set out in his Table 8.1 [D:B1997, pp. 7, 102-103]. Critical persons integrate all three domains at the highest levels [D:B1997, pp. 8, 104-105]. It is used to frame research and course design on student criticality [D:J2010; D:WH2016]. Its disputes, as later users read it: whether criticality is developed individually or emerges socially [D:WH2016], and whether it transfers across contexts [D:J2010]; Barnett himself calls the grid of levels and domains illegitimate but suggestive [D:B1997, p. 74].

objects.definition: A framework for critically reflective teaching: teachers hunt and check the assumptions behind their practice (paradigmatic, prescriptive and causal), especially those about power and hegemony, by looking at their teaching through four lenses: students' eyes, colleagues' perceptions, their own experience as learners and theory and research. Reach for it to make reflection critical rather than only descriptive, and to gather evidence from others about one's teaching. It is not a step-by-step cycle like Gibbs or Driscoll.
objects.extendedDefinition: Stephen Brookfield set out the framework in *Becoming a critically reflective teacher* (Jossey-Bass, 1995; 2nd edn 2017) [D:BR2017P; D:BR1995, not read]. Critically reflective teaching identifies and scrutinises the assumptions that shape practice, of three kinds (paradigmatic, prescriptive, causal); it is critical when it attends to assumptions about power and to hegemonic assumptions, which seem common sense but work against teachers' interests [D:BR2017P; D:LAN2018]. Teachers check their assumptions through four lenses: students' eyes, colleagues' perceptions, personal experience and theory [D:BR2017P; D:CUMB]. It is widely used in teacher development in higher and adult education [D:NWU2023]. Its disputes: Brookfield names problems without always offering remedies, and he warns that reflection forced against a framework becomes ritual [D:LAN2018]; a fifth lens, the learning environment, has been proposed for digital settings [D:KOS2025].

aliases: Fook and Gardner's critical reflection model
objects.definition: A group model of critical reflection on practice: each participant brings a concrete critical incident; in stage one the group's questions, drawn from four frameworks (reflective practice, reflexivity, postmodernism, critical social theory), unsettle the assumptions it reveals; in stage two, later, each person presents how their thinking has changed and what it means for practice. Reach for it to run critical reflection in supervision, teams or professional education, especially where power and assumptions matter. It is not a solo writing template.
objects.extendedDefinition: Jan Fook and Fiona Gardner set out the model in *Practising critical reflection: a resource handbook* (Open University Press, 2007), from Fook's earlier work on critical reflection in social work [D:BH2015; D:FG2007, not read]. It joins four theoretical foundations, reflective practice, reflexivity, postmodernism and critical social theory, and aims to reveal hidden assumptions and so empower practitioners, attending also to emotion [D:BH2015]. The process has two stages in a small group: unsettling assumptions through questioning about a concrete incident, then presenting changed thinking and its implications for practice [D:BH2015]; the authors later describe it as deconstruction and reconstruction and show it in health, social care, supervision, research and education [D:ANZ2013; D:FG2013, not read]. Studies find practitioners in supervision reflect, but seldom critically on the wider context [D:ANZS].

objects.definition: An expert-consensus account of critical thinking as purposeful, self-regulatory judgement, with two dimensions: six cognitive skills (interpretation, analysis, evaluation, inference, explanation, self-regulation) with sixteen sub-skills, and nineteen affective dispositions of the ideal critical thinker. Reach for it to name and describe critical thinking skills and dispositions in outcomes, teaching and assessment; and for its criteria for judging a critical thinking assessment. It is not a hierarchy or a sequence of skills: the panel says its order implies none.
objects.extendedDefinition: Peter Facione led a Delphi panel of 46 experts for the American Philosophical Association's Committee on Pre-College Philosophy from February 1988 to November 1989 and reported its consensus in 1990 [D:F1990, pp. 3-4, 7]. The panel defines critical thinking as "purposeful, self-regulatory judgment" yielding interpretation, analysis, evaluation and inference, with explanation of the considerations behind it, and describes the ideal critical thinker by habits of mind [D:F1990, p. 3]. It sets out six core skills with sixteen sub-skills (Tables 3 and 4) and nineteen affective dispositions (Table 5), with fifteen recommendations on teaching and assessment [D:F1990, pp. 3, 12-19, 25]. Its definition is among the most widely cited [D:AA2023], and it is the basis of tests of critical thinking skills and dispositions [D:H2022]. Its disputes: whether the dispositions belong to the meaning of critical thinking, on which the panel itself split about two to one [D:F1990, pp. 20-22]; and whether critical thinking is well conceived as skills and dispositions at all [D:B1998].

objects.definition: A leadership model for large, planned organisational change in eight stages: establish a sense of urgency, create the guiding coalition, develop a vision and strategy, communicate the change vision, empower broad-based action, generate short-term wins, consolidate gains and produce more change, and anchor new approaches in the culture; each stage answers one of eight common errors. Reach for it to plan or diagnose a major change, to test whether an effort has skipped a stage, or to explain why change is led more than managed. It is not a tested method: its author says it rests on what he has seen, not on published evidence.
objects.extendedDefinition: John Kotter set out eight errors that make corporate transformations fail in the Harvard Business Review of March-April 1995, and turned them into an eight-stage process in the book Leading Change in 1996, reissued with a new preface in 2012 [D:K2012, preface; new preface]. The stages run from establishing a sense of urgency to anchoring new approaches in the culture; they usually run in sequence though several run at once; large changes hold smaller projects each passing through all eight [D:K2012, ch. 2]. Kotter holds that successful transformation is mostly leadership, not management [D:K2012, ch. 2]. In 2014 he recast the stages as eight accelerators run concurrently by a volunteer network beside the hierarchy, a dual operating system [D:KA2014]. A review of fifteen years of literature found support for most steps but no study of the whole model [D:A2012]; Kotter himself says the book draws on no published source but his own [D:K2012, preface]; critics argue it has dated [D:H2016].

objects.definition: A theory that learning is the making of knowledge by transforming experience, in a cycle of four modes: concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation and active experimentation. Reach for it to design teaching, placements, simulations or reflective tasks that take learners round the whole cycle, and to plan the teacher's changing role. It is not a sound basis for sorting learners into fixed learning styles and teaching to them.
objects.extendedDefinition: Proposed by David Kolb in Experiential Learning (1984), drawing on the learning models of Lewin, Dewey and Piaget [D:K1984, pp. 20-25], and developed with Alice Kolb [D:KK2005; D:KK2017]. Kolb's working definition: "Learning is the process whereby knowledge is created through the transformation of experience" [D:K1984, p. 38]. Learners need four abilities, concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation and active experimentation, set on two opposed dimensions, and learning resolves the conflict between them [D:K1984, pp. 30-31]. [P2, 2 Oct: definition and modes from K1984.] Preferences among the modes form learning styles, four in the 1984 model and nine in the latest inventory [D:KK2005; D:KK2017]. It is used across higher, professional and management education to design learning round the cycle, and the authors map four teacher roles onto it [D:KK2017]. (editorial) Its main disputes: whether the cycle fairly reads its sources and describes how learning happens, and whether the learning style inventory measures anything stable [D:MOR2020; D:KF2002].

objects.definition: A style of software development for a whole team, built on five values (communication, simplicity, feedback, courage, respect), fourteen principles and practices such as weekly and quarterly cycles, stories, pair programming, test-first programming, continuous integration and incremental design. Reach for it when a team builds software against changing needs and wants engineering practices, short feedback loops and planning by scope, not just a planning framework. It is not a project portfolio, finance, operations or marketing method, and its author says it fails in organisations whose actual values contradict its own.
objects.extendedDefinition: Kent Beck first laid out XP's basics when he restarted Chrysler's C3 payroll project in 1996, with Ron Jeffries as its first full-time coach [D:BA2004, ch. 17], and set it out in Extreme Programming Explained (1999); he and Cynthia Andres rewrote the book in 2004 [D:BA2004, foreword to the second edition]. The 2004 account defines XP as a philosophy based on values, a body of practices that express them, complementary principles that bridge the two, and a community [D:BA2004, ch. 1]. It plans by scope in weekly and quarterly cycles, writes automated tests first and designs incrementally, and claims to address the risks of slipped schedules, cancelled projects, decaying systems, defects and misunderstood business needs [D:BA2004, ch. 1]. XP was the most studied agile method in the first decade [D:DD2008]. Its disputes: the evidence for it is of low strength [D:DD2008]; pair programming trades effort for quality or speed depending on the task [D:HDAS2009]; it was argued not to scale, though the 2004 edition claims it can [D:G2003; D:BA2004, ch. 1]; and accounts of its birth project's end differ (Part E item 2).

objects.definition: A framework of what students need in order to use feedback: four inter-related features (appreciating feedback, making judgements, managing affect and taking action), each with three descriptors, developed through peer feedback and analysing exemplars, with teachers designing the curriculum and coaching. Reach for it to design activities that build students' capacity to use feedback, to explain to students their part in the feedback cycle, or to plan feedback across a programme. It is not a guide for teachers' comments: it is about the students' side.
objects.extendedDefinition: David Carless and David Boud proposed a framework for student feedback literacy in 2018, extending Sutton's (2012) idea from reading written comments to the understandings, capacities and dispositions needed to make sense of and use information from any source [D:CB2018, pp. 1-2]. In this conceptual paper they review students' responses to feedback and the barriers to uptake, then propose four features: three inter-related ones (appreciating feedback, making judgements, managing affect) that together lead to the fourth, taking action [D:CB2018, pp. 2-5]. They show how peer feedback and analysing exemplars can develop it, with teachers designing the curriculum, guiding and coaching [D:CB2018, pp. 6-8]. They name the need for evidence on how comments lead to uptake, longitudinal and intervention studies, and work at postgraduate level and in the workplace [D:CB2018, p. 9].

objects.definition: Two models of feedback in higher education: Feedback Mark 1, where the teacher provides information on a task and checks that it changes a later task, and Feedback Mark 2, where learners seek, judge and use information from many sources, built into the curriculum and the learning milieu. Reach for it to explain the learning, assessment and feedback cycle, to design task sequences so feedback can be used, or to frame feedback as students' work rather than teachers' comments. It is not a guide to writing comments: the authors address curriculum design, not the microskills of giving feedback.
objects.extendedDefinition: David Boud and Elizabeth Molloy proposed two models of feedback in 2013, responding to student surveys in the UK and Australia that rate assessment and feedback below other features of courses [D:BM2013, ms pp. 1-2]. Mark 1 returns to feedback's origins in engineering: information counts as feedback only when a later performance shows its effect, so the loop must be completed [D:BM2013, ms pp. 6-8]. Mark 2, drawing on sustainable assessment and sustainable feedback, makes learners the drivers who seek and use information to inform their own judgements, and places feedback in the design of the curriculum and the learning milieu [D:BM2013, ms pp. 9-14]. The authors argue Mark 1 is too costly to sustain and keeps students dependent, while Mark 2 equips them beyond the course [D:BM2013, ms pp. 9, 20-21]. Its main limit, by the authors' own account, is that the models are conceptual: they leave implementation, trust and power to further study [D:BM2013, ms pp. 19-20].

objects.term: Seven principles of good feedback practice
aliases: seven principles of good feedback practice
objects.definition: A model of how students regulate their own learning through internal feedback, with seven principles of good feedback practice that strengthen that self-regulation, each with strategies teachers can use. Reach for it to audit or design a module's assessment and feedback, to explain why students must act on feedback, or to choose feedback strategies for large classes. It is not a model of teachers' comments alone: it treats the student as already generating feedback.
objects.extendedDefinition: David Nicol and Debra Macfarlane-Dick reinterpreted the research on formative assessment and feedback in 2006 to show how it can help students become self-regulated learners [D:NMD2006, p. 199]. They argue that feedback is still treated as transmission from teacher to student and set out four problems with that view [D:NMD2006, pp. 200-201]. Building on Butler and Winne (1995), they present a model in which a task set by the teacher triggers the student's own goals, strategies and internal feedback, with external feedback acting only through the student's interpretation [D:NMD2006, pp. 201-204]. From the model and the literature they derive seven principles of good feedback practice, each with strategies [D:NMD2006, pp. 205-215]. They propose that teachers audit their practice against the model and principles, and say the principles are a starting point to refine, not a complete set [D:NMD2006, p. 215]. The work came from the SENLEF project funded by the Learning and Teaching Support Network [D:NMD2006, p. 215].

aliases: Advance HE inclusive learning and teaching
objects.definition: A short sector framework that treats inclusive learning and teaching as a mindset and the foundation of quality, set out as three dials (institution, educators, students) of named conditions, each dial with one segment left blank for what we do not yet know. Reach for it to open a conversation with staff or students about inclusion in their own context, to frame a module or policy review, or to link inclusive practice to PSF evidence (Part F gives the dialogue). It is not a checklist or a compliance standard: it gives no procedure, measures or evidence base.
objects.extendedDefinition: Advance HE published the framework in 2024 as one of its Student Success Frameworks [D:AHE24, p. 2]. It defines inclusive learning and teaching as deliberately building approaches that let every student thrive, calls it the foundation of quality teaching and frames inclusion as a mindset rather than an end goal [D:AHE24, p. 2]. It names four things inclusion requires, addresses five audiences and looks at the subject from three perspectives, each drawn as a dial of named conditions with one segment left blank for unknown unknowns [D:AHE24, pp. 2-5, 12]. It sets self-actualisation of staff and students, mattering and psychological safety at its centre [D:AHE24, pp. 2, 10-11], gives each perspective three uses [D:AHE24, p. 12] and says inclusive practice is relevant to every PSF dimension [D:AHE24, p. 14]. Its main tension, which it names itself, is that inclusion is contested and often gatekept by existing policy and process [D:AHE24, pp. 2, 8].

objects.definition: A model of searching for information as six stages (initiation, selection, exploration, formulation, collection, presentation), each with typical feelings, thoughts and actions, in which uncertainty and anxiety rise in the early stages and fall once a focus is formed. Reach for it to explain why a student feels lost at the start of a search, to time help at each stage and to teach searching as a way of building understanding. It is not a search technique or a guide to sources: it describes the searcher's experience.
objects.extendedDefinition: Carol Collier Kuhlthau, at Rutgers, set out the Information Search Process in 1991 from five studies of library users, mostly students writing assigned papers, 558 participants in all [D:K1991, pp. 363-365; D:GEN2007, p. 80]. It treats searching as the user's construction of meaning, grounded in Kelly's personal construct theory, and models it in six stages, each with feelings, thoughts, actions and an appropriate task [D:K1991, pp. 362, 366-367]. Its central claim is that uncertainty, with its confusion and anxiety, is a natural part of the early stages, falling once a focus is formed [D:K1991, pp. 364, 369-370]. It is used in reference work, user education and school library programmes, and later as a basis for Guided Inquiry [D:GEN2007, pp. 82-83; D:KSITE]. Its disputes: it rests mostly on students with imposed tasks [D:GEN2007, p. 82], half its participants never formed a focus [D:K1991, p. 369]; and easy digital access tempts students to skip stages [D:KHT2008].

objects.definition: A short sector framework that treats internationalising higher education as an ongoing, institution-wide commitment to a globally aware and inclusive learning environment, set out as three dials (institution, educators, students) of named but undefined conditions, twenty in all. Reach for it to open a conversation with staff or students about what internationalisation means in their own context; it also helps frame a review of a module, programme or strategy and link that work to PSF evidence (Part F gives the dialogue). It is not a checklist, a standard or a recruitment strategy: it gives no procedure, measures, definitions of its segments or evidence base.
objects.extendedDefinition: Advance HE published the framework in 2024 as one of its Student Success Frameworks [D:AHE24I, p. 2]. It defines internationalising higher education as an ongoing commitment across the whole institution to a globally aware and inclusive learning environment, covering teaching, learning, research and knowledge exchange, and says it benefits every student whatever their location, background, discipline or mode of study [D:AHE24I, p. 2]. It addresses organisations and individuals within and beyond the sector, says it works best when applied at institutional level and embedded in programmes and looks at the subject from three nested perspectives, each drawn as a dial of named conditions [D:AHE24I, pp. 3, 5-11]. It gives each perspective three uses [D:AHE24I, pp. 12-13] and names eight PSF dimensions it is most relevant to [D:AHE24I, p. 14]. Its main tension is between internationalisation as a source of institutional standing and recruitment and internationalisation as an inclusive, reciprocal change in curriculum and culture [D:AHE24I, pp. 2, 4, 6]; it names no dispute itself.

objects.definition: A method for defining, managing and improving services that deliver knowledge work as a flow: make the work and its policies visible, limit work in progress so new work is pulled only when there is capacity, and improve the process by evolution from where it is now. Reach for it for continuous streams of work (support, operations, maintenance, service teams), to improve an existing process without reorganising it, or for flow metrics and probabilistic forecasting. It is not a project plan or a timeboxed delivery framework, and it requires no roles.
objects.extendedDefinition: David J. Anderson developed the Kanban Method from management approaches he used at Microsoft (reported in 2005) and Corbis; it was named in 2007 and set out in his book of 2010, which the authors call the method's seminal publication [D:EKC2016, pp. xi, 45]. It takes its name and one thread of inspiration from Toyota's kanban systems for limiting work in progress [D:EKC2016, p. xi]. It is a method for defining, managing and improving services that deliver knowledge work, built on nine values, three agendas, six foundational principles and six general practices, with a kanban system (a flow system with commitment and delivery points and WiP limits) at its centre [D:EKC2016, pp. 1-26]. It is used for software and other service work, alone or with Scrum [D:EKC2016, p. viii; D:SAN2018]. (editorial) Its evidence is mostly descriptive and positive, with few rigorous studies [D:AHM2018; D:SAN2018]; the authors themselves say survey use does not show effective use [D:EKC2016, p. viii]; and two bodies now publish different accounts of what Kanban is (Part E item 2).

objects.definition: A minimal definition of Kanban as a strategy for optimising the flow of value through any process: define and make visible the workflow, actively manage the items in it, improve it and track four flow metrics (WIP, throughput, work item age, cycle time). Reach for it when a team needs the smallest agreed core of Kanban, or flow metrics and forecasts to sit alongside another method such as Scrum. It is not Anderson's Kanban Method: it has no principles, values, cadences, roles or adoption approach.
objects.extendedDefinition: Written by John Coleman and Daniel Vacanti with contributors, first issued in July 2020 and revised in December 2020 and May 2025; it is published free at kanbanguides.org under a Creative Commons licence, which the current edition gives both as Attribution ShareAlike (p. 1) and as Attribution (p. 4) [D:KGH, pp. 1-4; D:KG2025, pp. 1, 4] (Part E item 2). It defines Kanban as a strategy for optimising the flow of value through a process, made of three practices working together: defining and visualising a workflow, actively managing items in it and improving it [D:KG2025, p. 1]. The explicit shared understanding of flow is the Definition of Workflow, with six minimum elements; four flow metrics are mandatory [D:KG2025, pp. 2-3]. It is meant to augment other value-oriented approaches [D:KG2025, p. 2]. (editorial) Its main dispute is what Kanban is: Kanban University's Kanban Method gives a wider, different account (run 0009), so "Kanban" may name either; the guide's site calls it the official, minimal reference and says Professional Kanban is defined completely in it [D:KGH, p. 1]; and published evidence on the guide itself is thin and mostly by its own authors (A7a).

aliases: Lean Software Development: An Agile Toolkit
objects.definition: Seven principles for applying lean thinking to software development (2003: eliminate waste, amplify learning, decide as late as possible, deliver as fast as possible, empower the team, build integrity in, see the whole; renamed in 2006), with the seven wastes of software and 22 thinking tools for translating the principles into agile practices. Reach for it to explain why agile teams limit work in progress, deliver in small batches and look at the whole value stream, or to map a value stream. It is not a cookbook of practices: the authors warn against adopting other teams' practices without thinking.
objects.extendedDefinition: Mary and Tom Poppendieck adapted lean manufacturing to software in Lean Software Development: An Agile Toolkit (2003): seven principles, one chapter each, and 22 thinking tools for leaders to design agile practices for their own setting [D:PP2003, pp. vii-xii, xxiv-xxvii]. They translate the Toyota Production System's seven wastes into seven wastes of software development, from partially done work to defects [D:PP2003, p. 4]; they close with instructions, a troubleshooting guide and a warranty valid only when all the principles are used [D:PP2003, pp. 179-186]. In 2006 they renamed the principles (eliminate waste, build quality in, create knowledge, defer commitment, deliver fast, respect people, optimise the whole) [D:PP2006X]. Its dispute is evidential: a review of lean in large-scale software found most studies non-empirical and focused on waste and flow [D:PGF2013].

objects.definition: A management framework of five principles for creating more value with less waste: specify value as the customer defines it, identify the value stream, make the value-creating steps flow, let the customer pull and pursue perfection by repeating the cycle; with an action plan for an organisation's lean leap over about five years. Reach for it to analyse and improve any repeated work that delivers something to a customer, and as the root of Kanban and lean software development. It is not a cost-cutting programme: the authors set it against downsizing and reengineering.
objects.extendedDefinition: James Womack and Daniel Jones set out lean thinking in 1996, after The Machine That Changed the World (1990) had named the Toyota way "lean production"; a revised edition followed in 2003 [D:WJ2003, pp. 5, 9]. Lean thinking is the antidote to muda, any activity that absorbs resources but creates no value; it has five principles: value, the value stream, flow, pull and perfection [D:WJ2003, pp. 15-26]. It generalises Taiichi Ohno's Toyota Production System, whose basis is the elimination of waste on the two pillars of just-in-time and autonomation [D:O1988, p. 4]. The authors give an action plan over five years [D:WJ2003, p. 270] and, in 2003, value stream mapping led by a value stream manager [D:WJ2003, pp. 316-321]. It spread from manufacturing to services, healthcare, public services and software [D:HHR2004; D:PP2003]. Its disputes: what lean is (no common definition [D:SW2007]), whether it fits work outside high-volume repetition, and its effects on staff and patients [D:HHR2004; D:HAS2012; D:MOR2016].

aliases: ten pieces of advice for student teams
objects.definition: A short student guide of ten numbered pieces of advice for a team of students doing a project together, from clarifying the brief and choosing members to running meetings, giving feedback and presenting, with checklists, a simplified team roles table after Belbin and a staged feedback exercise. Reach for it to give student teams practical, structured tools at the start of a group project, or to draft team-facing guidance on roles, ground rules, meetings and peer feedback on behaviour. It is not a theory of group development or an evidence review: it cites only Belbin and argues from practice.
objects.extendedDefinition: Graham Gibbs wrote the guide for the Oxford Centre for Staff Development, first published in 1993 and revised in 1994, as one of a series with a longer Student Manual of 27 exercises and a Tutor Guide [D:G1994, p. 1; PDF pages 2, 4]. Addressed to students, it holds that most difficulties of teamwork can be anticipated and overcome, and that teams gain most when all members read a section, discuss it and decide how to work, early on [D:G1994, p. 1]. Its ten pieces of advice run roughly in the order of a project: be clear about the task, choose members with care, build a real team, agree ground rules, allocate the crucial jobs, divide and share the work, hold proper meetings, review how it is going, give feedback gently and plan the team presentation [D:G1994, p. 1]. Its tools include a team roles table based on Belbin (1981), a meetings checklist, a checklist of team problems and guidelines for giving and receiving feedback [D:G1994, pp. 4, 10, 11, 13]. It reports no evidence of its own, and some of its language and media are of their time (Part E).

objects.definition: An eight-session group programme that teaches people who have recovered from recurrent depression to recognise and step out of the driven-doing mode of mind, in which low mood reactivates old patterns of ruminative thinking, into a being mode of direct, accepting awareness; the 3-minute breathing space is its spine. Reach for it to describe relapse prevention in recurrent depression, the doing and being modes and the structure of the course. It is not a treatment plan for anyone, it is not for acute depression, and it is not mindfulness in general.
objects.extendedDefinition: Zindel Segal, Mark Williams and John Teasdale developed MBCT in the 1990s, joining their account of why recovered patients relapse with Jon Kabat-Zinn's mindfulness-based stress reduction, and set it out in 2002 and 2013 [D:SWT2013, chs. 2-3]. Relapse, they hold, comes when lowered mood reactivates patterns of negative thinking from past episodes; the programme's core skill is recognising and disengaging from that driven-doing mode into a being mode in which thoughts are passing events [D:SWT2013, pp. 28-30, 68-74]. It runs as a pre-class interview, eight weekly classes of about twelve people, a day of practice and follow-up meetings, with daily home practice [D:SWT2013, pp. 82-83, 335-337; ch. 5]. In its first trial it nearly halved relapse for people with three or more past episodes, but not for those with two [D:SWT2013, ch. 19]. UK guidance names it, with group CBT, for relapse prevention [D:NICE2022, recs 1.8.5 and 1.8.6, p. 63]; a meta-analysis of nine trials found lower relapse against usual care and active treatments [D:KUY2016]. Its disputes: mixed results against structurally equivalent controls, trials run largely by its developers, and meditation-related adverse effects [D:MK2016; D:KUY2016; D:BRI2021].

objects.definition: A taxonomy of educational objectives: six levels of processing in three systems of thought (the cognitive system's retrieval, comprehension, analysis and knowledge utilisation, then metacognition, then self-system thinking), 21 mental operations under them, acting on three domains of knowledge. Reach for it to write and assess objectives that take in goal-setting, self-monitoring and motivation as well as thinking, or to build a 0 to 4 scale for a topic. Its levels are ordered by control and consciousness, never by difficulty.
objects.extendedDefinition: Robert Marzano proposed the New Taxonomy in 2001 as a work in progress; with John Kendall he revised it in 2007, and their 2008 handbook applies it to designing and assessing objectives [D:MK2007, preface; D:MK2008, p. 1]. It is offered as a replacement for Bloom's taxonomy [D:MK2008, p. 1]. Three systems of thought act on three domains of knowledge (information, mental procedures, psychomotor procedures); the systems are ordered by the flow of processing, which starts in the self-system, and the six levels by the conscious control they need, not by difficulty or complexity [D:MK2007, pp. 10-11, 16-17, 22, 60-61]. It is used to write objectives with a fixed stem, design assessments from generic probes for each level, clarify standards and plan curricula [D:MK2007, pp. 118-150]; the handbook adds scales of student performance on which a topic's expectation sits at 3.0 [D:MK2008, pp. 167-176]. Its disputes: whether objectives should address the metacognitive and self-systems at all (Hirsch, answered by the authors) [D:MK2007, pp. 121-122], and, from its evaluators, whether its three-tier control structure and hierarchy hold as stated [D:MOS2004; D:IRV2017].

objects.definition: A developmental map of an organisation's life in seven stages (Dreaming the Dream, Launching the Venture, Getting Organized, Making It, Becoming an Institution, Closing In, Dying), with transitions between stages and a path of renewal that loops back from Becoming an Institution through redreaming, recapturing the venture spirit and getting reorganised. Reach for it to read a team's or organisation's troubles as a stage passage rather than a problem to fix, and to plan renewal. It is not an empirically tested stage model: Bridges offers it as a working map.
objects.extendedDefinition: William Bridges set out the seven stages in *Surviving Corporate Transition* (1988) and in chapter 6 of *Managing Transitions* (2nd edition, 2003), reshaping Adizes's life cycle stages (1979) from his own consulting [D:BR2003, pp. 77, 95 notes 1, 2, 4; D:BR1988, not read; D:ADI1979, not read]. Transitions are the interludes between stages, closing one, renewing people in the neutral zone and carrying them into the next [D:BR2003, p. 82]. Five laws describe why each passage is resisted, and leaders can choose a path of renewal instead of Closing In [D:BR2003, pp. 83-85, 88-89]. It frames organisational development as development rather than repair; it applies to units and projects as well as whole organisations [D:BR2003, pp. 77, 92]. Its dispute: life cycle models are criticised as deterministic, and Bridges himself says the stages and names are not fixed [D:BR2003, p. 77; D:JB2018].

objects.definition: A humanistic talking therapy which holds that a person grows towards health when a therapist offers a relationship of genuineness, unconditional positive regard and empathic understanding that the client can perceive. Reach for it to describe or explain the core conditions, the non-directive stance and the theory behind them. Not for choosing anyone's treatment, and not a technique-based protocol.
objects.extendedDefinition: Carl Rogers developed it from the 1940s (recall: non-directive counselling, 1942), named it client-centred therapy in his book of 1951 (recall) and set out six necessary and sufficient conditions for therapeutic change in 1957 [D:CT2023; D:R1957]. Three of the six, the therapist's congruence, unconditional positive regard and empathy, are known as the core conditions [D:CT2023]. Empathy predicts client outcome moderately across orientations [D:ELL2018]. In the English IAPT service a person-centred experiential therapy did as well as CBT for depression at six months but less well at twelve [D:BAR2021]. (editorial) Its main dispute is Rogers's claim that the conditions are sufficient as well as necessary.

aliases: A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge
objects.definition: The Project Management Institute's standard guide to project management: in its 8th edition, six principles, seven performance domains and forty processes grouped in five focus areas; in its 7th, twelve principles, eight performance domains, tailoring and a catalogue of models, methods and artefacts, each published with The Standard for Project Management. Reach for it to describe what a project manager is expected to do and know across predictive, hybrid and adaptive approaches, and as the reference for PMI's certification. It is not a method with set roles and documents, as PRINCE2 is; it describes good practice to be tailored.
objects.extendedDefinition: The PMBOK Guide is the Project Management Institute's body of knowledge for project management, first piloted in 1983 [D:M2013, p. 53]. The 7th edition (2021) moved from a process-based standard to a principles-based one: twelve principles of project management guide behaviour, eight performance domains name the areas of work, and the guide adds tailoring and a catalogue of models, methods and artefacts [D:PMI2021G, Guide pp. 3-7, 227-230]. The 8th edition (November 2025, 408 pages) keeps that foundation but simplifies it to six principles and seven domains and reintroduces forty processes in a non-prescriptive form, grouped in five focus areas [D:PMI2025; D:BBK2026; D:LT]. It is used as the reference for PMI's certifications and as practice guidance [D:LT]. Its disputes: bodies of knowledge like it are poorly grounded in research and narrow in scope [D:SA2011; D:PW2016]; Morris argues it codified only the knowledge thought unique to project management and treats the work as execution and control rather than shaping the project's front end [D:M2013, pp. 54-55, 60]; and the 7th edition's move away from processes left practitioners without concrete steps [D:LT].

objects.definition: A process-based method for directing and managing a project in controlled stages: a project board authorises the project stage by stage against a business case, and a project manager runs each stage within tolerances on seven performance targets, escalating only exceptions. Reach for it where a project needs clear accountability across business, user and supplier, staged approval and governance records. It is not a delivery technique: it separates the management of the project from the specialist work, which any delivery method can do.
objects.extendedDefinition: PRINCE2 began as a UK government method (recall: PRINCE, from the CCTA, 1989; PRINCE2, 1996) and is now owned and published by PeopleCert, whose 7th edition, Managing Successful Projects with PRINCE2, appeared in 2023 [D:P2023; D:KT2023]. It is built from five integrated elements: seven principles, people, seven practices, seven processes and the project context [D:P2023, p. 3]. The principles are obligations: unless all seven are applied, it is not a PRINCE2 project [D:P2023, p. 4]. The project is planned, monitored and controlled stage by stage, with at least an initiation stage and a final stage, against tolerances on benefits, cost, time, quality, scope, sustainability and risk [D:P2023, pp. 7, 25-28, 214]. The 7th edition renamed the themes as practices, added the people element and sustainability, and reduced the management products to 15 [D:P2023, pp. 4, 286-287; D:KT2023]. It is used for projects that need formal control, in any sector and with any delivery method [D:P2023, pp. 10, 20]. Its disputes: whether its documentation outweighs its control where speed matters, and how far its effectiveness holds in practice [D:ZEL2025; D:WEL2012, pp. 43, 48].

objects.definition: The UK sector's framework of professional standards for teaching and supporting learning in higher education: 15 Dimensions (five Professional Values, five forms of Core Knowledge, five Areas of Activity) and four Descriptors (D1 to D4) of widening practice that map to Advance HE's Associate Fellow, Fellow, Senior Fellow and Principal Fellow. Reach for it to plan or evidence a teacher's or supporter of learning's professional development, to align an institution's development and recognition scheme, or to describe the dimensions of teaching practice. It is not a measure of teaching quality: recognition rests on written evidence of practice, and critics say it formalises more than it develops.
objects.extendedDefinition: Advance HE, GuildHE and Universities UK published the PSF in 2023, revising the UK Professional Standards Framework of 2011 [D:UKPSF2011, not read] after consulting over 800 people from more than 20 countries [D:PSF2023, p. 12; D:AHE2023]. Its 15 Dimensions inform and describe practice; four Descriptors set criteria against which individuals evidence their practice, each aligned with a category of Advance HE Fellowship [D:PSF2023, pp. 2, 4, 6-11]. Individuals use it to plan development and gain recognition, and institutions to build accredited development programmes and career pathways [D:PSF2023, pp. 6, 11]. Over 166,000 people hold Fellowship, 14,500 outside the UK [D:AHE2023]. Its disputes: studies of the UKPSF find recognition a retrospective, tick-box exercise driven by institutions, with little change to teaching [D:VDS2021; D:SHA2017].

objects.definition: A classification of learning outcomes for physical and practical skills. In Simpson's form it runs from perceiving the cues, through readiness and guided practice, to habitual, expert, adapted and finally original performance; in Harrow's it runs from reflexes, through fundamental patterns, perceptual and physical abilities, to skilled movement and expressive movement. Reach for it to write and sequence outcomes for practical, clinical, laboratory, craft or movement skills. It is not one agreed scheme: three rival taxonomies (Simpson, Dave, Harrow) use different levels, so name which one an outcome uses.
objects.extendedDefinition: The third domain of the Taxonomy of Educational Objectives was never published by Bloom's group; others filled the gap: Elizabeth Simpson (1966, revised 1972), R. H. Dave (1970) and Anita Harrow (1972) [D:K2002, p. 218; D:S1966; D:H1972, p. 8]. Simpson's 1966 report, written at the University of Illinois under a US Office of Education contract, orders the domain by complexity and the sequence of a motor act in five levels (perception, set, guided response, mechanism, complex overt response) and asks whether a sixth, adapting and originating, is needed [D:S1966, pp. 25-31]; by 1972 Harrow describes Simpson's model with seven levels, adding adaptation and origination [D:H1972, pp. 23-25]. Harrow's own taxonomy has six levels of observable movement: reflex movements, basic-fundamental movements, perceptual abilities, physical abilities, skilled movements and non-discursive communication [D:H1972, pp. 1-2, 32]. Dave's five levels run from imitation to naturalisation [D:D1970, not read; D:CLARK; D:RSDD2025]. It is used for practical skill outcomes in vocational, health, physical and engineering education and, recently, to classify tutoring systems [D:H1972, p. 10; D:RSDD2025]. Its disputes: which taxonomy to use, which of Simpson's versions a source means, and whether levels that cannot be observed belong in a scheme for objectives [D:UW; D:H1972, p. 24].

objects.definition: The model of a level-based qualifications framework as the UK uses it: a ladder of levels (FHEQ 4 to 8; FQHEIS within SCQF 7 to 12; CQFW Entry 1 to Level 8), each described by a qualification descriptor for its main award or by level descriptors in strands, setting threshold academic standards on an outcomes basis, with credit, typical qualifications and alignment to the European cycles. Reach for it to place a qualification or module at a level, to write or check outcomes against a level, or to compare levels across frameworks. It is not a subject standard: subject benchmark statements say what the levels mean in a discipline.
objects.extendedDefinition: The UK has two parallel frameworks for higher education qualifications, the FHEQ for England, Wales and Northern Ireland and the FQHEIS for Scotland, published together by QAA (2014; second edition updated 2024) [D:QF24, pp. 1, 4]. Each sets a hierarchy of levels and describes, for the main qualification at each level, the outcomes a holder must show: the national threshold academic standard [D:QF24, pp. 4, 7, 14]. Qualifications are awarded for demonstrated outcomes, not years of study [D:QF24, p. 7]. The FHEQ is part of Wales's wider Credit and Qualifications Framework (CQFW), whose level descriptors run from Entry 1 to Level 8 in three strands, and the FQHEIS is part of the SCQF [D:QF24, p. 9; D:CQ09]. The frameworks align with the European cycles and the EQF [D:QF24, pp. 8-9]. Their status differs by nation: required in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, while in England parts are adopted as the regulator's sector-recognised standards [D:QF24, pp. 4, 6].

aliases: Taking a strategic approach to managing quality and standards
Quality Code Principle 1 Advice and Guidance
strategic approach to managing quality and standards
objects.definition: QAA's non-mandatory Advice and Guidance for Quality Code Principle 1: what a provider-wide strategic approach to academic standards and quality looks like, unpacked across six Key Practices (responsibility, embedding, EEDI and sustainability, communication and governance, monitoring and evaluation, external expertise) with 67 reflective questions and six scenarios. Reach for it to design, document, govern or review a provider's quality framework and the evidence and reporting behind it. It is not a compliance checklist and does not interpret statutory requirements.
objects.extendedDefinition: QAA published this Advice and Guidance in July 2025 with a writing group of sector experts, peer reviewed across UK higher education, to unpack Sector-Agreed Principle 1 of the 2024 Quality Code and its six Key Practices [D:QAG1, pp. 1, 55]. It holds that effective oversight gives a provider a valid, systematic, evidence-based view of quality and standards at each level, used to enhance, share good practice, remedy issues, manage risk and allocate resources [D:QAG1, p. 4]. A strategic approach replaces piecemeal, overlapping arrangements with a coherent set of systems in one place, linked to the mission and strategic plan and approved by governors [D:QAG1, p. 4]. It sets out aims, key features, mechanisms, evidence and outputs (an annual report, analysis of qualitative feedback, a live dashboard), then guidance per Key Practice with reflective questions and a scenario each [D:QAG1, pp. 2, 5-7]. It is illustrative, not mandatory; regulators do not treat it as compliance indicators [D:QAG1, p. 1]. Its main tension, which it names itself, is between a shared sector view and each provider's own context: quality is not homogeneity [D:QAG1, p. 1].

aliases: Quality Code Principle 2 Advice and Guidance
objects.definition: QAA's sector-agreed, non-mandatory guidance on Principle 2 of the Quality Code: how a provider engages students as active partners in assuring and enhancing quality, through six Key Practices on strategy, representation, demonstrating impact, inclusion, recognition and governance. Reach for it to design or review a student engagement strategy, a representation system, a practice for closing the feedback loop, a recognition and reward scheme or support for student governors. It is not about engagement in learning or attendance monitoring: those belong to Principle 11 and are outside its scope.
objects.extendedDefinition: QAA published this Advice and Guidance in July 2025, written with a group of sector experts and peer reviewed across UK higher education, to unpack Principle 2 of the 2024 Quality Code and its six Key Practices [D:QAG2, p. 1]. The principle asks providers to take deliberate steps to engage students individually and collectively as active partners in quality at all levels of decision making and to act on and report the enhancements that result [D:QAG2, p. 3]. The guidance sets this against transactional approaches [D:QAG2, p. 4] and works through strategy and culture, representation and the student voice, closing the feedback loop, inclusion, recognition and reward and governance, each with reflective questions and scenarios [D:QAG2, pp. 7-46]. Providers use it to benchmark and enhance their practice; it is not mandatory and regulators do not treat it as compliance indicators [D:QAG2, pp. 1-2]. Its main tension, which it names itself, is between partnership as the preferred approach and the fact that not all students want to or can engage that way [D:QAG2, p. 19].

aliases: Resourcing delivery of a high-quality learning experience
Quality Code Principle 3 Advice and Guidance
objects.definition: QAA's non-mandatory, sector-written guidance on Principle 3 of the UK Quality Code: how a provider plans, secures, maintains and evaluates the staff, spaces, technology, learning resources and services behind a high-quality learning experience, set out in seven Key Practices with reflective questions and scenarios. Reach for it to review resource planning against the student journey, to test whether learning environments and resources are accessible, inclusive and sustainable; or to check that staff development and quality processes are properly resourced. It is not a costing method or a compliance test: it sets no figures, ratios or thresholds.
objects.extendedDefinition: QAA published this Advice and Guidance in September 2026, written with a group of sector experts and peer-reviewed across UK higher education, to unpack Sector-Agreed Principle 3 of the 2024 Quality Code [D:QAG3, pp. 1, 3]. The principle asks providers to plan, secure and maintain learning, technology, facilities and staffing resources for an accessible, innovative, high-quality learning experience that fits their strategy and student body [D:QAG3, p. 5]. The guidance treats resourcing as a chain from a governing-body-approved strategy through strategic and operational plans to in-year allocation, anchored in the evidenced needs of students along the whole student journey [D:QAG3, pp. 7-12]. Its seven Key Practices cover planning; dedicated and inclusive resources; review and update; staff development; resourcing quality processes; accessible and inclusive learning environments; monitoring and evaluation. Each Key Practice has reflective questions and one or two scenarios [D:QAG3, pp. 2, 5]. It is illustrative rather than mandatory; regulators and QAA do not treat it as compliance indicators [D:QAG3, p. 3]. Its main tension is with finance: it asks for broad investment while conceding that action on feedback must sit within the available resource envelope [D:QAG3, p. 56].

aliases: Using data to inform and evaluate quality
Quality Code Principle 4 Advice and Guidance
objects.definition: QAA's non-mandatory guidance on Principle 4 of the UK Quality Code: how providers collect, govern, share and analyse qualitative and quantitative data to inform quality decisions and then evaluate what difference those decisions made, across six Key Practices (strategy, awareness, ethics and data protection, staff training including generative AI, partnership data sharing agreements and data that serves diverse students). Reach for it to build or review a provider's data strategy, data governance, data sharing agreements, data training or disaggregated EDI and sustainability analysis. It is not a statement of data protection law and not a compliance test: it summarises the law only as context and leaves statutory duties to the provider.
objects.extendedDefinition: QAA published this Advice and Guidance in September 2026, written with a writing group of sector experts and peer reviewed across UK higher education, to unpack Principle 4 of the 2024 Quality Code and its six Key Practices [D:QAG4, pp. 3, 6]. Its central claim is that collecting data and acting on it is not enough: providers should evaluate the impact of their changes, in ways that can be light, embedded in everyday work and proportionate to their size [D:QAG4, p. 7]. For each Key Practice it gives practical approaches, tables, figures, reflective questions and two scenarios, and it closes with a glossary of 36 terms [D:QAG4, pp. 4, 11-94]. Its main uses are a provider's data strategy, governance and ownership, awareness and trust, lawful and ethical monitoring, staff data literacy, data sharing agreements with partners and the student representative body, and disaggregated analysis that responds to diverse students [D:QAG4, pp. 11-87]. It is advisory: regulators and QAA do not treat it as compliance indicators [D:QAG4, p. 3]. No published critique was read.

aliases: Quality Code Principle 5 Advice and Guidance
objects.definition: QAA's sector-written, non-mandatory guidance on Principle 5 of the 2024 Quality Code: how a provider agrees principles for monitoring and evaluation, documents its methods, trains and engages staff and students, communicates outcomes, evaluates the impact of its own enhancements, uses monitoring for EDI and sustainability and feeds external review into programme and module review. Reach for it to design or review an annual monitoring and periodic review framework, to choose an evaluation approach (Theory of Change, logic model, risk-based, performance measurement) or to plan the evaluation of an enhancement project. It is not a compliance checklist and does not interpret statutory or regulatory requirements.
objects.extendedDefinition: QAA published this Advice and Guidance in September 2026, written with a group of sector experts and peer-reviewed across UK higher education [D:QAG5, pp. 3, 79, 81]. It unpacks Principle 5, that providers regularly monitor and review their provision with students, staff and external expertise and consider the outcomes at provider level, and its seven Key Practices (a to g) [D:QAG5, p. 6]. It defines monitoring as routine tracking while provision runs and evaluation as planned assessment of effectiveness and impact [D:QAG5, p. 7], sets out three approaches to monitoring and four to evaluation [D:QAG5, pp. 9-13] and then treats each Key Practice with advice, reflective questions and scenarios [D:QAG5, pp. 16-77]. Its recurring themes are proportionality, an evaluative mindset over compliance and closing the loop by evaluating the enhancements themselves [D:QAG5, pp. 7, 17, 51, 55]. It is advisory: neither QAA nor the national regulators treat it as compliance indicators [D:QAG5, p. 3]. No dispute is recorded in the source; no critique was read.

aliases: Engaging in external review and accreditation
Quality Code Principle 6 Advice and Guidance
Engaging in external quality and standards review and accreditation
objects.definition: QAA's non-mandatory Advice and Guidance on Principle 6 of the 2024 Quality Code: how a provider builds external review and accreditation (regulatory review, provider-commissioned review and PSRB accreditation) into its strategy, turns the outcomes into enhancement, resources the people who take part, understands the UK regulatory and legislative context and prepares for review in partner delivery locations.
