Reach for it to plan review readiness, to set up post-review action planning or to prepare a partnership for in-country review or accreditation. It is not a review method or a regulator's handbook: it interprets no statutory requirement and sets no pass or fail criteria.
objects.extendedDefinition: QAA published this guidance in September 2026 with a writing group of sector experts, peer-reviewed across UK higher education, to unpack Principle 6 and its five Key Practices [D:QAG6, pp. 3, 5]. It treats three types of external review (regulatory review and monitoring, provider-commissioned review and PSRB accreditation) and two internal reviews with an external element that support them, and leaves charter marks and pledges out of scope [D:QAG6, pp. 7-8]. Its central argument is that engagement with review must go beyond showing compliance: a narrow focus breeds "compliance fatigue", while treating each review as organisational learning builds a resilient quality culture [D:QAG6, p. 6]. Each Key Practice has practical considerations, reflective questions and scenarios; two figures model the support staff need and the stages of a partnership [D:QAG6, pp. 4, 27, 41]. It is advisory: regulators and QAA do not read it as compliance indicators [D:QAG6, p. 3]. No published critique was read; the guidance itself names the risks of tick-box engagement and the resource it demands [D:QAG6, pp. 6, 24].

aliases: Quality Code Principle 7 Advice and Guidance
objects.definition: QAA's non-mandatory Advice and Guidance on Principle 7 of the 2024 Quality Code: how providers design, develop, approve and modify programmes and modules so that standards match the qualifications frameworks, set out under seven Key Practices (reference points and PSRB requirements, definitive documents, award records, published processes, external engagement, EDI and sustainability, student involvement). Reach for it to design or review a provider's programme approval and modification process, to prepare for validation or to decide what a definitive programme document should hold. It does not state the academic standards themselves (the qualifications frameworks and subject benchmark statements do) and it leaves out early decisions on a programme's viability.
objects.extendedDefinition: QAA published this guidance in September 2026 with a writing group of sector experts, peer reviewed across UK higher education, to unpack Sector-Agreed Principle 7 and its seven Key Practices [D:QAG7, pp. 3, 5]. The principle asks providers to design, develop, approve and modify programmes and modules so that quality and the standards of awards match the relevant qualifications framework and are comparable across the UK and with the European framework [D:QAG7, p. 5]. Degree-awarding bodies hold ultimate responsibility, exercised through providers' own processes [D:QAG7, p. 6]. The guidance treats design as creative and iterative, describes a typical cycle from outline proposal to validation and final approval, and sets risk-based modification beside it [D:QAG7, pp. 13, 15-17]. Each Key Practice ends with reflective questions and scenarios for self-review [D:QAG7, p. 4]. It is explicitly not a compliance test, and it warns readers not to equate quality with uniformity across providers [D:QAG7, p. 3].

aliases: Quality Code Principle 8 Advice and Guidance
objects.definition: QAA's non-mandatory Advice and Guidance for Quality Code Principle 8: how providers and their partners keep standards secure and enhance quality in provision delivered with others, unpacked across six Key Practices (shared responsibility, due diligence and risk, written agreements, compliance and cultural context, partnership records, ongoing monitoring and evaluation) with 64 reflective questions and nine scenarios, plus a typology of partnership and collaborative arrangements. Reach for it to approve, document, record, run, review or close a partnership, franchise, validation, joint award, articulation, placement or TNE arrangement. It is not legal advice and does not interpret statutory requirements.
objects.extendedDefinition: QAA published this Advice and Guidance in July 2025 with a writing group of sector experts, peer reviewed across UK higher education, to unpack Sector-Agreed Principle 8 of the 2024 Quality Code and its six Key Practices [D:QAG8, pp. 1, 54]. Principle 8 covers every arrangement in which two or more organisations deliver teaching, learning, assessment or support, from whole programmes to placements, single modules, progression routes and shared services [D:QAG8, p. 4]. It holds that partnership should add value without prejudice to standards or the student experience and that its quality arrangements should be as rigorous and open to scrutiny as single-provider provision; all partners share responsibility, but the awarding body stays ultimately accountable for its awards [D:QAG8, p. 4]. It sets out due diligence scaled to risk (with a risk continuum and an approval matrix), what a written agreement must cover through to closure, legal and cultural differences in other countries and the UK nations, the records to keep and publish and a cycle of monitoring and evaluation [D:QAG8, pp. 11-15, 20-22, 26-35, 37-38, 42-44]. It is illustrative, not mandatory; regulators do not treat it as compliance indicators [D:QAG8, p. 1]. Its main tension, which it names itself, is between proportionate arrangements fitted to each partner and arrangements as rigorous as the awarding body's own [D:QAG8, pp. 4, 6].

aliases: Quality Code Principle 9 Advice and Guidance
objects.definition: QAA's non-mandatory, sector-written guidance on Quality Code Principle 9: how a UK provider runs fair, transparent and inclusive recruitment, selection and admissions and keeps applicants accurately informed, set out under four Key Practices with 52 reflective questions and 8 scenarios. Reach for it to review an admissions policy, selection criteria, applicant information, admissions training or the handling of course changes during a cycle. It is not a statement of consumer or equality law and not a compliance test: it does not interpret statutory requirements.
objects.extendedDefinition: QAA published this Advice and Guidance in September 2026 with a writing group of sector experts, peer-reviewed across UK higher education, to unpack Sector-Agreed Principle 9 of the 2024 Quality Code and its four Key Practices [D:QAG9, pp. 3, 41]. It reads the principle as matching each course with the students able to succeed on it, through evidence-led processes and honest information from first contact to enrolment [D:QAG9, pp. 6-7]. The four Key Practices cover fair and transparent admissions policies (a), information that supports applicants and their advisers (b), training and resourcing of everyone who recruits and admits (c) and clear, consistent communication along the applicant journey, including when programmes change (d) [D:QAG9, p. 5]. Each Key Practice gives practical considerations, then reflective questions and two scenarios for self-review [D:QAG9, p. 4]. Its main use is benchmarking and enhancing a provider's admissions practice; its main tension, visible in its scenarios, lies between recruitment pressure and fair, transparent selection [D:QAG9, pp. 14, 20, 35]. It is explicitly not mandatory and not a set of compliance indicators [D:QAG9, p. 3].

aliases: Supporting students to achieve their potential
Quality Code Principle 10 Advice and Guidance
objects.definition: QAA's non-mandatory Advice and Guidance for Quality Code Principle 10: how a provider builds a framework of support around a mapped learning journey, with five Key Practices on information, transitions, awareness of services, staff capability and activities beyond the curriculum. Reach for it to design or review a provider's student support, transition or communication arrangements, or to prepare evidence against Principle 10. It is not a compliance test and not guidance on teaching and assessment, admissions or complaints, which have their own principles.
objects.extendedDefinition: QAA published this guidance in September 2026 with a writing group of sector experts, peer-reviewed across UK higher education, to unpack Principle 10 of the 2024 Quality Code and its five Key Practices [D:QAG10, pp. 3, 5, 68]. It opens with the framework of support and the learning journey on which it rests, with an example journey map and the student groups that may need targeted support [D:QAG10, pp. 6-11]. It then takes each Key Practice in turn: information for students and staff; support at transition points; awareness and use of services; qualified, trained and supported staff; and the value of activities outside the formal curriculum [D:QAG10, pp. 14-62]. Each section ends with reflective questions and illustrative scenarios for self-review [D:QAG10, p. 4]. It is illustrative rather than mandatory and regulators do not treat it as compliance indicators [D:QAG10, p. 3]. It cites no research for its claims; no published evaluation was read.

aliases: Quality Code Principle 11 Advice and Guidance
QAA teaching learning and assessment guidance
objects.definition: QAA's sector-agreed Advice and Guidance on Quality Code Principle 11: how a UK provider makes teaching, learning and assessment collaborative, inclusive and aligned, through eight Key Practices on scholarship and alignment, information and feedback, qualified staff and research environments, the student's role, transitions, assessment design, digital technologies (including GenAI) and academic integrity. Reach for it to review or design a provider's assessment, feedback, GenAI or academic integrity policy, or to test a programme against the Key Practices with its 119 reflective questions and 15 scenarios. It is not a compliance checklist and does not interpret statutory duties such as the Equality Act.
objects.extendedDefinition: QAA published this guidance in September 2026, written with a writing group of sector experts and peer-reviewed across UK higher education, to unpack Sector-Agreed Principle 11 of the 2024 Quality Code [D:QAG11, pp. 3, 96]. The principle asks providers to take a collaborative and inclusive approach that lets all students progress and develop academic and professional skills, with varied assessment grounded in academic integrity and outcomes comparable across the UK [D:QAG11, pp. 5, 7]. The guidance treats each of its eight Key Practices in turn, with practical considerations, reflective questions and scenarios [D:QAG11, p. 4]. Its main uses are to design constructively aligned and inclusive assessment, to plan feedback and feedforward, to set coherent approaches to technologies such as GenAI and to build an academic integrity framework [D:QAG11, pp. 10-11, 22-23, 74, 86]. It is advisory: neither QAA nor the national regulators treat it as compliance indicators [D:QAG11, p. 3]. Its live tensions are flexibility against comparability in assessment and the line between permitted and prohibited GenAI use [D:QAG11, pp. 60, 64, 87, 89].

aliases: Quality Code Principle 12 Advice and Guidance
Quality Code complaints and appeals guidance
objects.definition: QAA's non-mandatory guidance on Principle 12 of the UK Quality Code: how providers run concerns, complaints and appeals processes that are accessible, fair and clear, resolve cases early and in proportion, meet the oversight bodies' rules and feed outcomes back into enhancement. Reach for it to design, review or benchmark a provider's complaints and appeals procedures, to distinguish a concern from a complaint from an appeal, or to plan how case outcomes reach governance. It is not a statement of the ombudsmen's requirements or of the law: it points to the OIA, SPSO, NIPSO and CMA and does not interpret statute.
objects.extendedDefinition: QAA published the Advice and Guidance for Sector-Agreed Principle 12 in September 2026, written with a group of sector experts and peer-reviewed across UK higher education [D:QAG12, pp. 1, 3]. It unpacks the principle that providers run robust, fair, transparent and accessible processes for complaints and appeals, review them and use the outcomes for enhancement [D:QAG12, pp. 5-6]. It separates concerns (early, informal issues), complaints (dissatisfaction with a service, an act or treatment, not academic judgement) and appeals (a review of how a decision was made) [D:QAG12, p. 6]. Six Key Practices cover accessible and inclusive processes, clear stages, the oversight bodies' requirements, proportionate action and early resolution, monitoring and review and the use of outcomes, each with reflective questions and scenarios [D:QAG12, pp. 5, 9-47]. Providers use it to benchmark and enhance their own procedures; it is not mandatory and regulators and QAA do not treat it as compliance indicators [D:QAG12, p. 3]. Its main tension is national: the Scottish model complaints procedure has no informal stage, so the guidance's early informal resolution reads differently in Scotland [D:QAG12, p. 12].

objects.definition: A model of how reflection turns experience into learning: from an experience, the learner returns to it, attends to the feelings it raised and re-evaluates it by association, integration, validation and appropriation, leading to outcomes such as new perspectives, changed behaviour and commitment to action. Reach for it to explain or assess the processes of reflection, especially the place of feelings, and to code reflective writing. It is not a template of headings for a single write-up like Gibbs or Driscoll.
objects.extendedDefinition: David Boud, Rosemary Keogh and David Walker set out the model in *Reflection: turning experience into learning* (Kogan Page, 1985) [D:MT; D:BKW1985, not read]. It has three parts: experiences; reflective processes (returning to the experience, attending to feelings, re-evaluating the experience through association, integration, validation and appropriation); and outcomes (new perspectives, change in behaviour, readiness for application, commitment to action) [D:MT]. It aims to turn unplanned action into self-aware action through structured reflection [D:MT]. Researchers use its elements to code the depth of students' reflections, as a longitudinal study of software engineering apprentices did [D:BNA2025]. Its disputes: the stages overlap and are less distinct in practice than in the model by the authors' own account; coders also find its categories hard to tell apart [D:MT; D:BNA2025].

objects.definition: A structured way to reflect on an experience, moving in order through description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusions and an action plan for next time. Reach for it to scaffold a reflective account, a debrief after practice or simulation, or a reflective essay, above all in nursing, health and teacher education. It is not a theory of learning in its own right: Gibbs set it out as a debriefing structure for Kolb's cycle, and used alone it can produce descriptive rather than critical reflection.
objects.extendedDefinition: Graham Gibbs set out the cycle in Learning by Doing (1988), a guide to teaching and learning methods written with Bob Farmer and Diana Eastcott for the Further Education Unit [D:G1988, PDF pp. 2-3, 7]. It is the "structured debriefing" of section 4.3.5: seven stages (description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, general and specific conclusions, personal action plans) mapped onto Kolb's experiential learning cycle, which the book adopts as its theory [D:G1988, PDF pp. 14-15, 49-50]. It became widely used in health care, staff development and teacher education [D:G1988, PDF p. 6; D:FONS2015]. Most later accounts give six stages, merging the two conclusions [D:HULL; D:G1988, PDF p. 3]. Its main dispute: used as a template, it can yield superficial reflection with no critical analysis [D:HULL; D:TOL2023].

objects.definition: Schön's account of how professionals know and learn in practice: competent practice rests on tacit knowing-in-action; when practice surprises them, practitioners reflect-in-action, reframing the problem and testing the frame by moves that also change the situation, in a reflective conversation with it. Reach for it to explain what reflective practice is, why professional education uses studios, supervision and reflection; it is also the source of most reflective models. It is not a step-by-step reflective model like Gibbs's; it describes how practitioners think.
objects.extendedDefinition: Donald Schön (1930-1997) argued in The Reflective Practitioner (1983) that technical rationality, the view of professional practice as instrumental problem solving made rigorous by applying scientific theory, cannot account for the uncertainty, instability, uniqueness and value conflict of real practice, and that competent practitioners rely instead on tacit knowing-in-action and on reflection-in-action [D:S1983, pp. 21, 39-40, 49-50; D:INFED]. Reflection-in-action is a reflective conversation with the situation: the practitioner frames the problem, experiments by moves that also probe and test, and reframes on the situation's back-talk [D:S1983, pp. 79, 131-132]. Educating the Reflective Practitioner (1987) proposed the practicum to teach it [D:INFED]. It underpins reflective practice in teaching, nursing and social care [D:EAT; D:ASH1996]. Its disputes: whether reflection-in-action is possible when time is short, whether the concept has content, and whether formal assessment of reflection undermines it [D:INFED; D:ASH1996; D:EAT]; Schön himself answers the first [D:S1983, pp. 276-278].

objects.term: Atkins and Murphy's model of reflection
aliases: Atkins and Murphy's model of reflection
objects.definition: A nursing model of reflection with three stages (awareness of uncomfortable feelings and thoughts, critical analysis of feelings and knowledge, a new perspective) and five skills it needs (self-awareness, description, critical analysis, synthesis, evaluation); its 1994 form is a cycle of describing, analysing, evaluating the relevance of knowledge, identifying learning and acting. Reach for it to name the skills reflection asks of a learner and to move a reflection from feelings to a changed perspective. It is not a broad theory of learning from experience like Kolb's.
objects.extendedDefinition: Sue Atkins and Kathy Murphy set out the model in a review of the literature on reflection in the *Journal of Advanced Nursing* (1993) [D:KOO2011; D:AM1993, not read]. Reflection begins with awareness of uncomfortable feelings and thoughts, moves to critical analysis of feelings and knowledge, and ends in a new perspective; it calls on self-awareness, description, critical analysis, synthesis and evaluation [D:KOO2011]. In *Nursing Standard* (1994) they set it out as a cycle: describe the situation, analyse feelings and knowledge, evaluate the relevance of knowledge, identify learning and act in a new experience [D:FONS; D:AM1994, not read]. It is used in nursing and health education and is taught beside Gibbs and Kolb [D:FONS; D:OU]. No published critique was reached in this pass (Part E).

aliases: Rolfe's what so what now what
objects.definition: A three-level reflective framework from nursing: a descriptive level (What?), a theory- and knowledge-building level (So what?) and an action-orientated, reflexive level (Now what?), each with cue questions that push from describing an incident to drawing on knowledge and wider issues and planning action. Reach for it when reflection should connect practice to theory and to broader issues while staying short. It is not a research method of reflexivity (items 35 to 37), though it borrows the word.
objects.extendedDefinition: Gary Rolfe, Dawn Freshwater and Melanie Jasper set out the framework in *Critical reflection for nursing and the helping professions: a user's guide* (Palgrave, 2001), taking Borton's three questions and turning them into three levels of reflection [D:BASEL; D:UOW; D:RFJ2001, not read]. The descriptive level asks what happened and one's part in it; the theory- and knowledge-building level asks what it means, what one's actions were based on, what other knowledge applies and what broader issues arise; the action-orientated, reflexive level asks what to do, with its consequences and planning [D:BASEL]. Teaching guides present it as simple and adaptable across disciplines and career stages [D:UOW]. Its dispute is the shared one of reflective models: whether short question frames support critical depth; no study of its effects was found.

objects.definition: A critical review that separates three meanings of "reflexivity" in social work: an individual's considered response to their context and life choices (after Giddens and Beck); a self-critical questioning of how knowledge is produced and how power works in its production; and attention to the part emotion plays in practice. It also sets reflexivity apart from reflection, critical reflection, reflectivity and critical reflectivity, chiefly by timing (in the moment against after the event) and by whether insight is held to generalise. Reach for it to say which meaning of reflexivity a course or practice intends. It is not a method or stage model.
objects.extendedDefinition: Heather D'Cruz, Philip Gillingham and Sebastian Melendez reviewed social work literature since the 1990s and found "reflexivity" used without clarity about who should be reflexive, when and how, often interchangeably with reflection and critical reflection [D:DGM2007, pp. 73-74]. They identify three variations of meaning: reflexivity as an individual's response to context and choices; as a self-critical approach to how knowledge is generated and how power operates in it; and as concerned with emotion in practice [D:DGM2007, p. 75]. Critical reflection differs from reflexivity mainly in timing, reflecting on a past incident rather than questioning in the moment, and in claiming that its insights generalise [D:DGM2007, pp. 83-84]. Each variation takes social work in a different direction, from individual change to social change [D:DGM2007, pp. 86-87]. The authors see the lack of clarity as part of theory development but a cause of confusion, notably in assessing students' reflection [D:DGM2007, pp. 74, 85].

objects.definition: A conceptual framework, not a rubric, for making research skills explicit and developing them coherently from primary school to PhD: six facets of research (embark and clarify, find and generate, evaluate and reflect, organise and manage, analyse and synthesise, communicate and apply), each with a key question and an affective facet, set against five degrees of student autonomy, from prescribed to unbounded research, with a researcher version that adds adopted and enlarging research. Reach for it to design tasks, outcomes and marking by facet and autonomy across a course or programme, to plan collaboration between academics, librarians and learning developers, or to connect research skills with problem solving, academic literacy and work skills (the MELT family). It is not a research methods guide and its levels are not years of study.
objects.extendedDefinition: John Willison and Kerry O'Regan devised the Research Skill Development (RSD) framework in 2006 at the University of Adelaide and published it in 2007 [D:W2018, pp. 1, 15; D:WO2007]. It started from the six information literacy standards of ANZIIL (Bundy 2004) combined with Bloom's taxonomy, with SOLO informing analyse and synthesise [D:W2018, p. 1]. Each facet is set against a continuum of student autonomy, which describes how much guidance educators give, not a student's year of study [D:W2018, pp. 1, 5]. After twelve years of critique, the 2018 version renamed and regrouped the facets, renamed the autonomy levels and rewrote cells; it also added an affective facet and a key question for each facet [D:W2018, pp. 4-8]. Evidence comes from 29 courses in five universities and several degree-programme studies, mostly by Willison and colleagues [D:W2018, p. 6]. Critics question whether its continuum fixes power relations and whether frameworks over-structure research learning [D:W2018, pp. 5, 8].

objects.definition: A two-dimensional classification of learning objectives: what kind of knowledge an objective concerns (four types) and what the learner is to do with it (six cognitive process categories, nineteen processes). Reach for it to classify, write or check the alignment of objectives, activities and assessments; not for affective or psychomotor objectives.
objects.extendedDefinition: A revision of the 1956 Taxonomy of Educational Objectives (Bloom and colleagues), produced by a group led by Lorin Anderson and David Krathwohl and published in 2001 [D:AK2001]. It splits the original's single scale into two dimensions: a knowledge dimension (factual, conceptual, procedural, metacognitive) and a cognitive process dimension (remember, understand, apply, analyse, evaluate, create), so that an objective, read as verb plus noun, is placed in one or more cells of a 4 by 6 taxonomy table [D:K2002, pp. 213-215]. Category names became verbs; synthesis became create and moved to the top; the strict cumulative hierarchy of the original was relaxed to allow overlap [D:K2002, p. 214; D:AK2001, pp. 265-268]. Its main stated uses are classifying objectives and checking that objectives, activities and assessments align [D:K2002, pp. 213, 215-217]. (editorial) It is the most widely used taxonomy for writing learning outcomes in higher education; its ordering by complexity and its use of verb lists are both contested (A7).

objects.definition: A lightweight framework for a small, self-managing team to deliver a complex product in short fixed cycles (Sprints), inspecting and adapting the product and the way of working at set events. Reach for it to plan or run iterative product work; not for fixed-scope, low-uncertainty work, and not as a full project-management method (it says nothing about budgets, contracts or portfolios).
objects.extendedDefinition: Defined by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland in The Scrum Guide, first published in 2010 and last revised in November 2020 [D:SG2020]. Scrum rests on empiricism and lean thinking: work is made transparent, inspected and adapted in fixed-length Sprints of a month or less. It specifies one team of three accountabilities (Developers, Product Owner, Scrum Master), five events and three artifacts, each artifact with a commitment [D:SG2020, pp. 3-12]. The Guide calls the framework immutable: using only parts of it is not Scrum [D:SG2020, p. 13]. (editorial) It is the most widely used agile framework in software and increasingly outside it; most organisations adapt it, and whether adaptation is tailoring or erosion ("ScrumBut") is the main dispute (A5d).

objects.definition: A developmental model of how college students and young adults move from uncritical reliance on external authority, through a crossroads, to self-authorship (the internal capacity to construct their own beliefs, identity and social relations), with the Learning Partnerships Model of three supports and three challenges that educators use to promote it. Reach for it to design teaching, advising or student affairs work that develops students' internal voice, or to explain to students why being asked what they think matters. It is not an assessment instrument: it gives no way to place an individual student on the journey.
objects.extendedDefinition: Marcia Baxter Magolda summarised her account of self-authorship in a 2014 chapter, drawing on a 27-year longitudinal study of young adults from age 18 to 45 and the Wabash National Study [D:BM2014, p. 26]. Building on Kegan (1994), she defines self-authorship as the internal capacity to construct one's beliefs, identity and social relations. She argues that college must develop it so graduates can meet adaptive challenges [D:BM2014, pp. 25-26]. She portrays a journey across cognitive, intrapersonal and relational dimensions from uncritically following external formulas, through a crossroads, to self-authorship [D:BM2014, pp. 26-30]. The Learning Partnerships Model, which emerged from the same study, names three ways learning partners support learners' internal voices and three ways they challenge them [D:BM2014, pp. 30-31]. She notes that most graduating seniors have not yet reached self-authorship [D:BM2014, p. 27] and calls for research on reshaping college environments, peer culture and educators' own development [D:BM2014, p. 31].

aliases: phases and areas for self-regulated learning
four phase by four area taxonomy
objects.definition: A map of self-regulated learning as four phases (forethought, monitoring, control, reaction and reflection) crossed with four areas a learner can regulate (cognition, motivation and affect, behaviour, context), with a two by two taxonomy of goal orientations (mastery or performance, approach or avoidance) and what each predicts for those processes. Reach for it to locate a study skill, intervention or research question within self-regulation, or to reason about how students' purposes for a task shape how they monitor and control their learning. It is not a teaching procedure: the phases are a heuristic, not a sequence to follow.
objects.extendedDefinition: Paul Pintrich wrote this chapter in 2000 with two aims: to give a synthetic framework for the many models of self-regulated learning, and to show how goal orientation, as a motivational construct, links to self-regulation [D:P2000, pp. 451-452]. He sets out four assumptions the models share and a working definition [D:P2000, pp. 452-453], then a table of four phases by four areas for regulation and discusses each of its sixteen cells [D:P2000, pp. 453-472]. In the second part he separates target goals from goal orientations, reviews the models of goal orientation and proposes a taxonomy of mastery and performance goals in approach and avoidance forms [D:P2000, pp. 472-479]. He reviews the research linking each to self-regulation: approach-mastery goals are generally adaptive, avoidance-performance goals maladaptive, approach-performance goals mixed, and avoidance-mastery goals a new and untested proposal [D:P2000, pp. 479-490]. He closes with six directions for research, including measurement, moderators, multiple goals, automaticity, context and culture [D:P2000, pp. 490-494].

objects.definition: Seven research-based principles of good teaching practice in undergraduate education: student and staff contact, cooperation among students, active learning, prompt feedback, time on task, high expectations and respect for diverse talents and ways of learning, which together draw on six forces (activity, cooperation, diversity, expectations, interaction, responsibility). Reach for it to review or design teaching, a module or an institution's environment for learning, or to frame staff development. It is not a curriculum model: the authors address how to teach, not what.
objects.extendedDefinition: Arthur Chickering and Zelda Gamson, with a group of US higher education researchers, set out seven principles of good practice in the *AAHE Bulletin* in March 1987, sponsored by the American Association for Higher Education and the Education Commission of the States [D:CG1987, pp. 3, 4]. They rest the principles on 50 years of research on teaching, learning and student life; each works alone but their effects multiply together [D:CG1987, p. 4]. Each principle comes with examples from US colleges, and the article closes with what institutions, states and accreditors can do to support good practice [D:CG1987, pp. 4-6]. The principles became among the most cited frames for undergraduate teaching and were later adapted to technology (Chickering and Ehrmann 1996, recall). The authors themselves name a limit: they offer no view on curriculum content [D:CG1987, p. 4].

aliases: habits of mind heart and hand
objects.definition: Shulman's theory that each profession has characteristic forms of teaching, its signature pedagogies, which prepare novices to think, perform and act with integrity, and which can be read at three levels (surface, deep and implicit structure) plus what they leave out. Reach for it to analyse or design the core teaching of a professional or disciplinary programme, to name what that teaching forms in students, or to borrow a pedagogy from another profession. It is not a teaching method to apply: it is a lens for seeing a field's habitual teaching and its costs.
objects.extendedDefinition: Lee Shulman, then president of the Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching, set out the idea of signature pedagogies in a 2005 essay drawing on the Foundation's studies of preparation for the professions [D:S2005, pp. 52-53]. Signature pedagogies are the characteristic types of teaching that organise how future practitioners are educated, in the three dimensions of professional work: thinking, performing and acting with integrity [D:S2005, p. 52]. He illustrates them with law's case dialogue, medicine's clinical rounds and engineering's design studio, analyses them by surface, deep and implicit structure and by what they omit, and names their shared features: pervasive routine, public performance, accountability, uncertainty and emotional stakes [D:S2005, pp. 52-58]. He warns that the habits which make them powerful also make them rigid, proposes the idea of compromised pedagogy where one dimension of practice is subordinated, and names the conditions that can change them [D:S2005, pp. 56-59]. No published critique was read this pass (W-0270).

objects.definition: A non-hierarchical taxonomy of six interacting kinds of significant learning (foundational knowledge, application, integration, human dimension, caring, learning how to learn), with a twelve-step model for designing a college course around them: analyse the situation, then set three parts that support one another (learning goals; feedback and assessment; teaching and learning activities). Reach for it to write course goals beyond knowing and applying and to design or check a whole course. It is not a ladder of levels like Bloom's: its kinds support each other rather than rise.
objects.extendedDefinition: L. Dee Fink, for decades director of the University of Oklahoma's instructional development programme, set out the taxonomy of significant learning and integrated course design in Creating Significant Learning Experiences (2003; revised and updated 2013) [D:F2013, pp. vii-ix, xvii]. Defining learning as change, he names six kinds of significant learning that are relational and interactive, not hierarchical, offered as a broader set of goals than Bloom's cognitive taxonomy [D:F2013, pp. 33-38]. The design model sets three decisions (learning goals; feedback and assessment; teaching and learning activities) on an analysis of situational factors and asks that they be integrated, in twelve steps over three phases [D:F2013, pp. 69-75]. Fink sees it as essentially the same procedure as backward design and constructive alignment [D:F2013, pp. 69-71]. Its weakness is evidential: studies of it are single-course redesigns without comparison groups [D:CAN2024].

objects.definition: A theory that learning is taking part in the practice of a community: newcomers learn by legitimate peripheral participation, moving from limited but genuine tasks at the edge towards full membership, and change who they are as they do. Reach for it to explain or plan learning on placement, in apprenticeship, at work or in any practice a student joins. It is not a teaching method or a lesson design: its authors offer it as a way to analyse learning, not as a pedagogy.
objects.extendedDefinition: Jean Lave, an anthropologist, and Etienne Wenger set out situated learning in *Situated learning: legitimate peripheral participation* (Cambridge University Press, 1991), drawing on five studies of apprenticeship: Yucatec midwives, Vai and Gola tailors, US Navy quartermasters, meat cutters and non-drinking alcoholics in Alcoholics Anonymous [D:CUP; D:SMITH]. They argue that learning is a social process, not only something in the learner's head, and that its defining process is legitimate peripheral participation in a community of practice [D:CUP; D:NL]. Learning is a change of identity as well as of knowledge [D:COX2005]. The theory is used across workplace, professional and health professions education, often to study placements and to design communities of practice [D:FHHU2005; D:OBB2020]. Its disputes: whether it accounts for power, conflict and institutions [D:COX2005; D:CW2003; D:FHHU2005], and whether it may be used as a design, since its authors say it is not a pedagogy [D:NL; D:WIKI; D:OBB2020].

aliases: Structure of the Observed Learning Outcome
objects.definition: A taxonomy of five levels for judging the structure of a learner's response, from missing the point (prestructural) through one, then several unconnected relevant aspects, to an integrated whole (relational) and a generalisation beyond what was given (extended abstract). Reach for it to judge the quality of answers, to write graded rubrics and to set intended learning outcomes at a chosen depth with its verbs, as constructive alignment does. It does not classify affective or psychomotor outcomes, and a verb alone does not fix a level.
objects.extendedDefinition: Proposed by John Biggs and Kevin Collis in Evaluating the Quality of Learning (1982) [D:B1982], from the analysis of school students' answers to open questions in several subjects [D:MARG2019; D:BD2009, p. 4], after Biggs had already graded learning outcomes by structural complexity [D:B1979]. It names five levels of increasing structural complexity: prestructural, unistructural, multistructural, relational and extended abstract; the first steps add relevant aspects (quantitative growth), the last two integrate and then generalise them (qualitative change) [D:BD2009, pp. 4-5]. The authors tie the levels to Piaget's stages but place them on the response, not the learner [D:B1982, pp. 22-23]; in 1991 they set the levels as a learning cycle that recurs within each of five modes [D:BC1991, pp. 62-67]. It began as a way to assess the quality of learning beyond marks [D:ADN2022] and became, through Biggs's constructive alignment, a source of verbs for intended learning outcomes [D:BIG2009 via run 0003; D:BD2009, pp. 4-5]. (editorial) Its main disputes: whether a level can be fixed reliably, by raters from an answer (the authors report interjudge correlations of .71 to .95 [D:B1982, pp. 188-190]) or by anyone from a verb [D:ADN2022; D:BD2009, pp. 8, 14].

objects.definition: A set of cue questions for reflecting on a significant experience: first "looking in" to one's thoughts and feelings, then "looking out" through cues grouped by Carper's patterns of knowing (aesthetics, personal, ethics, empirics) with reflexivity added to link the experience to past and future practice. Reach for it when a nurse or other practitioner needs a values-aware structure deeper than Gibbs's six stages, above all within guided reflection with a supervisor. It is not a form to complete in order: its author calls the cues devices to help reflection, and they differ between editions.
objects.extendedDefinition: Christopher Johns, a nurse, built the model for structured reflection (MSR) by analysing the dialogue between practitioners and guides in the guided reflection he began at Burford in 1989, and revised it through use: by 2000 it was in its 12th edition [D:J2000, pp. 34, 46]. The 2000 version asks the practitioner to look in, paying attention to thoughts and feelings, then look out: describe the situation, name the significant issues and answer cues grouped as aesthetics, personal, ethics, influencing factors, empirics and reflexivity [D:J2000, p. 47]. Johns tuned the cues to Carper's patterns of knowing (1978) but says the framing has educational, not practical, value [D:J2000, pp. 48, 78]. Later editions add an opening cue, "bring the mind home" [D:NOTT], and the sixth edition of the book (2022) revises the model significantly [D:J2022]. It is used in nursing, health professional education and clinical supervision [D:J2000, p. 44; D:HVDHB]. Its disputes: that structured cyclic models push reflection into retrospect [D:JPP2018], and, as Johns himself warns, that the cues are grasped as a technology and used in concrete ways [D:J2000, pp. 48-49].

objects.definition: A longitudinal theory of why students leave or stay: students arrive with attributes, goals and commitments, which their experience of a college's academic and social systems strengthens or weakens through academic and social integration, and the resulting commitments decide whether they persist. Reach for it to frame student transition, retention and belonging across the student life cycle, and, in Tinto's later form, to plan action on self-efficacy, belonging and the perceived value of the curriculum. It is not a predictive instrument: its propositions have mixed empirical support.
objects.extendedDefinition: Vincent Tinto set out the model in a 1975 synthesis of research on dropout and developed it in *Leaving College* (1987; 2nd edn 1993), drawing on Durkheim's account of suicide and van Gennep's rites of passage [D:AL2016; D:TIN1975, not read; D:TIN1993, not read]. Students enter with pre-entry attributes and with commitments to the goal of graduating and to the institution; their experience of the academic and social systems produces academic and social integration, which reshapes those commitments and so the decision to stay or leave [D:AL2016; D:SCH2014]. Tinto later moved the theory towards institutional action [D:TIN2012, not read] and then to the student's own motivation to persist, shaped by goals, self-efficacy, sense of belonging and the perceived value of the curriculum [D:T2017; D:TIN2019]. It is among the most used frames for retention research and practice [D:AL2016; D:SCH2014]. Its disputes: only part of its propositions find robust support, and integration may not suit non-traditional, commuter and minority students or may ask them to leave their identity behind [D:AL2016; D:SCH2014; D:PPRC2010].

objects.definition: The model behind QAA's Subject Benchmark Statements: sector-owned, non-regulatory reference points, written by academics for each subject, that describe a degree's purposes, distinctive features, content and delivery; they set benchmark standards at threshold (and often typical and excellent) for honours and sometimes master's graduates, with cross-cutting themes such as EDI, accessibility, sustainability, enterprise and, from 2026, generative AI. Reach for it to understand how a statement is built and used in course design, validation, review and external examining; or to read any one statement correctly. It is not a subject's standards themselves, nor a national curriculum.
objects.extendedDefinition: QAA publishes Subject Benchmark Statements on behalf of the UK higher education sector; each is written by an advisory group of subject academics and defines what a graduate in the subject might know, do and understand at the end of their studies [D:PS23, p. 1; D:QSB, summary]. They are an established part of quality assurance but not a regulatory requirement, and their status varies by nation: not sector-recognised standards in England, a key reference point in Wales and Scotland, and part of quality requirements in Northern Ireland [D:PS23, pp. 1-2]. The current editions (2022 to 2026) share a revised structure: context and purposes with cross-cutting themes; distinctive features; content, structure and delivery; benchmark standards [D:PS23, p. 1; D:UREF]. Providers use them to design, approve and review courses, external examiners to judge comparability, and professional bodies to read academic standards [D:PS23, p. 1; D:SO26, p. 1]. Their limit, by their own account, is that they guide rather than prescribe: the awarding provider holds responsibility for standards [D:PS23, pp. 1-2].

aliases: Taxonomy of Educational Objectives Handbook I
objects.definition: A classification of intended learning outcomes in the cognitive domain into six ordered categories (knowledge, comprehension, application, analysis, synthesis, evaluation), each but application with numbered subcategories, made in 1956 to help examiners share test items. Reach for it to read older curricula, tests and outcome statements written against it, or to compare with the 2001 revision. For writing new outcomes, prefer the revision (run 0001), which most current guidance uses; and do not treat the order of the top categories as settled.
objects.extendedDefinition: Initiated by Benjamin Bloom, then Associate Director of the University of Chicago's Board of Examinations, to make it easier for universities to exchange test items measuring the same objective; a group of measurement specialists met about twice a year from 1949 and published the handbook in 1956 [D:K2002, p. 212; D:B1956]. It orders six categories from simple to complex and concrete to abstract, assumed to form a cumulative hierarchy in which each is prerequisite to the next [D:K2002, pp. 212-213]. It became widely known, was translated into 22 languages and was used above all to classify curricular objectives and test items [D:K2002, p. 213]. Its disputes: the knowledge category is unlike the others, mixing content and process; "understand" was left out; and whether the hierarchy holds, above all the order of synthesis and evaluation, which the 2001 revision swapped [D:K2002, pp. 213-215; D:FUR1981].

objects.definition: A programming discipline with two rules: write new code only when an automated test has failed, and remove duplication; worked in a cycle of minutes from red (a failing test) to green (passing) to refactor, from a list of tests. Reach for it to describe or coach a test-first way of writing code, the step sizes it allows and the patterns that keep the cycle going. It is not a testing strategy for a whole system: its author says it does not replace performance, stress or usability testing.
objects.extendedDefinition: Kent Beck set out test-driven development in Test-Driven Development: By Example (2002; copyright 2003), having called it test-first programming within Extreme Programming. Its goal is clean code that works; its two rules are to write new code only if an automated test has failed and to eliminate duplication; they imply the order red, green, refactor [D:B2003, pp. ix-x]. Beck presents it as a way of managing fear and of controlling the gap between a decision and its feedback, and gives some 70 patterns for choosing, writing and passing tests and for refactoring [D:B2003, pp. xi-xii, 121-192]. Its main dispute is evidence: Beck himself says no study has shown its effect and rests on anecdote [D:B2003, pp. 202-203]; reviews find research results contradictory because studies differ [D:GHA2020], and a study of professionals found that small, steady steps mattered for quality and productivity while writing the test first did not [D:FUC2017].

objects.definition: A three-stage account of planned change: loosen the current way of working (unfreeze), move to the new one, then make it stick (refreeze). Reach for it to describe the simplest and most cited model of organisational change, or the origin that later models such as Kotter's elaborate. Not a detailed plan, and not safely attributed to Lewin in that form without noting the dispute.
objects.extendedDefinition: In section 6 of a 1947 article in the first issue of Human Relations, published just after his death, the social psychologist Kurt Lewin wrote that a successful change has three aspects: unfreezing the present level if necessary, moving to the new level and freezing group life at the new level, so that the new force field is secure against change [D:L1947, pp. 34-35; D:CBB2016, p. 35]. He offered it as the way planned social change "may be thought of" and argued that group decision serves all three better than individual instruction [D:L1947, p. 36]. Later writers, Lippitt and colleagues (1958) and Schein (from 1961), turned the passage into a staged model for change agents and renamed the last step refreezing [D:CBB2016, pp. 41-42]; it is now taught as the foundation of change management [D:CBB2016, p. 34]. Its main dispute is that foundation: Cummings, Bridgman and Brown show the idea takes two short paragraphs in Lewin's work, with no evidence or illustration, and argue the model is a post hoc reconstruction [D:CBB2016, pp. 35-37]; Burnes replies that it was a well-thought-out part of his field theory [D:BUR2020]. [P2, 2 Oct: rewritten from L1947 and CBB2016.]

objects.definition: A model of how people go through change inwardly: change is the outer situation, transition the inner psychological process of coming to terms with it, which runs through an ending, a confused in-between "neutral zone" and a new beginning, three processes that overlap. Reach for it to plan how a leader helps people let go of the old, get through the neutral zone and make a new beginning during an organisational change, using the author's tactics, checklists, readiness audit and monitoring team. It is not a plan for the change itself and is not tested by research; pair it with a model of the change.
objects.extendedDefinition: William Bridges (1933-2013) set out the model for life transitions in Transitions (1980; second edition 2004) and for organisations in Managing Transitions (1991; second edition 2003; later editions with Susan Bridges) [D:BR2004, preface; D:BR2003; D:HAC2017; D:HAC2019]. It separates change, which is situational, from transition, the psychological three-phase process by which people come to terms with the new situation: an ending, a neutral zone and a new beginning [D:BR2003, pp. 3-5]. The phases go on at the same time and are better seen as three processes, all needed for a transition to finish [D:BR2003, pp. 9, 100-101]. Managers use it to plan support for people through each phase, often beside Kotter's or Lewin's models [D:BR2003, chapters 3-5; D:MT; D:MIL2017]. Its main dispute: it rests on the author's consulting experience, not on research; critics fault its likeness to the Kübler-Ross change curve and its universal account of emotional response [D:HB2025].

aliases: UK Quality Code for Higher Education
objects.definition: The UK-wide, sector-led reference point for securing academic standards and assuring and enhancing quality in higher (and tertiary) education: twelve Sector-Agreed Principles in three groups, each with Key Practices (73 in all), supported by non-mandatory Advice and Guidance. Reach for it to map or evaluate a provider's quality framework, to prepare for review or to find which principle governs an area of practice (design and approval, partnerships, admissions, support, teaching and assessment, complaints). It is not regulation in England and not a statement of academic standards for a level or subject: those are the qualifications frameworks and subject benchmark statements.
objects.extendedDefinition: QAA published the fourth version of the UK Quality Code for Higher Education in June 2024, developed with the sector and aligned with the European Standards and Guidelines (ESG) [D:QC24, p. 1]. It has two elements, twelve Sector-Agreed Principles and the Key Practices under each, supported by Advice and Guidance [D:QC24, pp. 1, 4]. The principles fall in three groups: a strategic approach (1 to 3), evaluating quality and standards (4 to 6) and implementing the approach (7 to 12) [D:QC24, pp. 4-15; D:QCP]. Providers use it to build their own quality frameworks, to review policy and practice, to enhance the student experience and to promote equality, diversity and inclusion and environmental sustainability [D:QC24, pp. 2-3]. Its status varies: a key reference point in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, voluntary in England except under Educational Oversight Review [D:QC24, p. 2]. The Advice and Guidance is explicitly not a compliance test [D:QAG, summary].

objects.definition: A map of five ways researchers practise reflexivity, the continuing, self-aware evaluation of how they shape their research: introspection, intersubjective reflection, mutual collaboration, social critique and discursive deconstruction, each with its own opportunities and pitfalls. Reach for it to choose and justify a reflexive approach in qualitative research, and to teach the difference between reflection after the event and reflexivity during it. It is not a model for reflecting on practice in general; its home is research.
objects.extendedDefinition: Linda Finlay set out five variants of reflexivity in "Negotiating the swamp" (*Qualitative Research*, 2002), likening the researcher to an explorer crossing a swamp of endless deconstruction, self-analysis and self-disclosure [D:FIN2002S; D:FIN2002SA]. In "'Outing' the researcher" (*Qualitative Health Research*, 2002) she defines reflexivity as continuing, conscious self-awareness of one's responses, relationships and the research process, distinguishes it from reflection, and shows it at work before, during and after data collection [D:FIN2002O]. Each variant offers different opportunities and challenges, so researchers choose their path [D:FIN2002SA]. It is widely cited in qualitative research and in the teaching of reflexive practice [D:EJQ]. Its disputes: reflexivity can slide into infinite regress, self-indulgent navel-gazing that privileges the researcher, and positivist dismissal as bias [D:FIN2002O].

objects.definition: A three-question model of reflection: What? (describe what happened), So what? (work out what it means) and Now what? (decide what to do next), each with trigger questions, used most in nursing and clinical supervision. Reach for it when a short, memorable frame for reflecting on an experience is needed, often with a supervisor or peer. It is not a deep or critical model: it leaves critique of assumptions and context to the reflector.
objects.extendedDefinition: Terry Borton posed three questions, What?, So what? and Now what?, in *Reach, touch and teach* (1970); John Driscoll adapted them for nursing in 1994 and in his books on clinical supervision (2000; 2nd edn 2007), adding trigger questions to each stem and tying the stems to the stages of an experiential learning cycle [D:NOTT; D:EBS2024; D:POLYU; D:BOR1970, not read; D:DRI1994, not read; D:DRI2007, not read]. It is valued for being short and easy to remember, and is used in nursing, healthcare, supervision, careers work and service learning [D:EBS2024; D:MARCR]. Its limits, by comparison with other models: it is less structured than Gibbs's cycle or Johns's cues and is not the most widely used (run 0032; [D:EBS2024]); no study of its effects was found.

objects.definition: A practice framework for student group work in higher education: thirteen linked topics around a core of benefits and challenges, learning to work in a group and assessing group work, gathering named tools (Tuckman's stages, Belbin's roles, the PETS process, CATME-BARS, mark redistribution, partnership values) with advice for diversity, delivery mode, pedagogy, discipline, roles, space and strategy. Reach for it to design, support or assess a group project, to answer free-riding or fairness worries, or to plan the progression of teamwork skills across a programme. It is not a theory of group development or team roles: for those it relies on models read only through it.
objects.extendedDefinition: Mick Healey wrote this evidence-based review and guide in July 2024 for the University of Westminster's teaching innovation centre, drawing on almost 200 references, for staff who use group work, academic developers and those who set programme and institutional strategy [D:H2024, pp. 1, 11]. It focuses on student project teams that work together for at least several weeks [D:H2024, pp. 11-12] and is organised by a thirteen-part framework whose core is benefits and challenges, learning to work in a group and assessing group work [D:H2024, p. 13]. Its argument is that group work has an important role in learning but works only when designed for its context [D:H2024, p. 17]. It recommends explicit learning outcomes for teamwork, considered team selection and size, support through stages of team development, team roles, a response to free-riding that explores its causes, assessment of process as well as product through peer and self-assessment with redistributed group marks, inclusion framed as equity and justice and a programme-wide strategy for progression [D:H2024, pp. 18-35]. Its main tension, which it states itself, is that the stage and role models it uses were built for business and transfer imperfectly to student groups [D:H2024, pp. 12-13, 22, 27].
